comments.text: Measured 2026-08-24 against the binary built from agent/bd-jlv68: 'ntm --robot-status --session does-not-exist' returns success:true, exit 0, with sessions:[] — it accepts an unknown session scope and answers as though it had filtered. The scoped --robot-snapshot landed by bd-jlv68 is strictly stricter: same input returns success:false, error_code SESSION_NOT_FOUND, exit 1. So scoping --robot-status here must also make an unknown session an error, not an empty success; the two aggregates disagreeing is how the silent-wrong-scope defect survives in a second shape.

title: SLB approvals key on agent identity, not the OS user — usable on a single-login machine
description:
## Outcome

SLB approvals work on a single-login machine: requester/approver identity is the AGENT identity
(AGENT_NAME / session actor / an explicit --as), not the OS user — so a human at the keyboard
can approve a request made by an agent session under the same login, and the two-operator
control protects something instead of deadlocking.

## Context

Measured 2026-08-31 (o62l shakedown): a force-release of two orphaned file reservations
(ids 861/862, held by an abandoned pane, blocking the last legitimate bead's commit) produced
approval requests; the human operator's `ntm approve <id>` was rejected with "SLB violation:
approver cannot be the same as requester" — both resolve to the login user. On this machine
every actor is the same $USER (the br claim-guard hit the identical wall), so the only paths
were the blanket `ntm policy automation --force-release auto` (defeats the control) or waiting
out the TTL. A safety gate that cannot ever pass on the deployment it targets is a gate that
gets toggled off.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Requester identity recorded from the agent identity (AGENT_NAME or session actor) when
  present, falling back to OS user only when absent.
- [ ] An approve from a different agent identity (or an explicit human `--as` identity) under
  the same OS user is accepted; an approve from the SAME agent identity is still rejected
  (the control survives).
- [ ] The single-login deadlock case is covered by a test.

## Recovery path

Identity-resolution change only; the SLB flow is otherwise untouched.

comments.author: drive-beads-c4ba2d16
comments.text: Second wall behind the first, same incident: with 'ntm policy automation --force-release auto' toggled ON by the human, the operator-shell force-release still failed — agentmail requires a registration_token for the CLI's assumed agent ('AmberCove') unless the MCP session already authenticated as it. So neither the two-operator path (self-approval deadlock) nor the solo-operator toggle is usable from an operator shell; only a registered agent session can force-release, and the abandoned holder is by definition not around to do it. The operator released directly in the store (UPDATE released_ts), which is what the TTL would have done at expiry. Acceptance should add: an operator-shell path (human at the keyboard) can force-release with the policy toggle on, without impersonating a registered agent.

title: Refuse the tmux isolation bypass unless TMUX_TMPDIR proves the caller owns a server
description:
## Outcome

Test isolation can no longer be defeated by an ambient environment variable.
`NTM_TEST_TMUX_ENV_OWNED=1` is honoured only when the process that sets it really does own an
isolated tmux server — proven by `TMUX_TMPDIR` pointing at a test temp root — and is ignored
otherwise, falling back to isolating normally. A `go test` run started from a shell that
happens to export the variable no longer runs every real-tmux test against the developer's
own tmux server.

## Context

`tests/testutil/throttle.go:221-224` returns a no-op cleanup the moment
`NTM_TEST_TMUX_ENV_OWNED=1` is present in the process environment: the private `TMUX_TMPDIR`,
the `TMUX`/`TMUX_PANE` clearing at `:237-247` and the scoped `kill-server` cleanup at
`:252-277` are all skipped. `internal/tmux/session_test.go:17-20` carries a hand-copied
duplicate of the same check, guarding that package's own inline `TestMain`
(`session_test.go:17-92`).

Between the two copies, one exported variable disables isolation for `internal/cli`,
`internal/checkpoint`, `internal/robot`, `internal/tmux`, `e2e` and `tests/e2e` at once. With
isolation off and no `TMUX_TMPDIR` in the environment, tmux resolves its default socket, so
every `kill-server` and `KillSession` in those packages targets the host's live server —
including the ones that tear down a whole server, such as `throttle.go:256`,
`session_test.go:69` and the per-test cleanups in `internal/pipeline` and
`internal/tui/dashboard`.

The variable exists for a real reason and is not being removed. Seven sites re-exec the test
binary as a helper and must not have the child create a second isolated root:
`internal/tmux/session_test.go:373-378`, `:540-544`, `:613-617`,
`internal/tmux/extra_test.go:172-176`, `internal/cli/assign_test.go:4204-4208`, and
`internal/cli/scale_test.go:364-368`, `:423-429`. Every one of them builds `cmd.Env` by
extending `os.Environ()`, so the parent's already-isolated `TMUX_TMPDIR` reaches the child by
inheritance. That inheritance is the invariant the guard can verify instead of trusting the
flag, which is what makes this fixable without touching any of the seven.

No script, Makefile target or CI workflow in the repo exports the variable
(`git log -G"NTM_TEST_TMUX_ENV_OWNED" -- scripts/ Makefile .github/` is empty), so the only
way it reaches a `go test` invocation is a shell that kept it from an earlier command — which
leaves no trace in the failure and no trace in the repo.

The two copies of the check have already drifted, which is why converging the predicate is in
scope: `session_test.go:94-99`'s `tmuxTestTempBase()` honours neither the
`NTM_TMUX_TEST_TMPDIR` override nor the 100-byte socket-path limit that `throttle.go:36-43`
enforces. Converging the rest of that duplicate `TestMain` is deliberately **not** in scope.

Rejected: deleting the variable. The seven helper sites would each then build an isolated root
inside a process whose parent already has one, and the child's `kill-server` cleanup would
race the parent's.

## Steps to Reproduce

```sh
tmux new-session -d -s bystander
export NTM_TEST_TMUX_ENV_OWNED=1
unset TMUX_TMPDIR
go test ./internal/tmux/ -run TestSessionLifecycleReal
tmux has-session -t bystander        # exits non-zero: the session is gone
```

The suite's own cleanup killed the default server. The same reproduction works against
`./internal/cli/`, `./internal/checkpoint/` and `./internal/robot/`, because all four reach
the guard through the same helper.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A single exported predicate in `tests/testutil` decides whether the caller owns an
      isolated server. It returns true only when `TMUX_TMPDIR` is non-empty and its base name
      matches the `ntm-tmux-test-*` pattern from `throttle.go:43`.
- [ ] `IsolateTmuxTestProcess` (`throttle.go:221`) consults that predicate instead of reading
      `NTM_TEST_TMUX_ENV_OWNED` directly. When the variable is set but the predicate is false,
      it isolates as if the variable were unset and writes one line to stderr naming both the
      variable and the resolved `TMUX_TMPDIR`.
- [ ] `internal/tmux/session_test.go:17-20` calls the same predicate rather than repeating the
      literal check.
- [ ] All seven helper re-exec sites listed in Context still pass with their `cmd.Env` lines
      unchanged: `go test ./internal/tmux/ ./internal/cli/` is green.
- [ ] Done when: with `NTM_TEST_TMUX_ENV_OWNED=1` exported and `TMUX_TMPDIR` unset, the
      reproduction above leaves the `bystander` session alive.

## Tests

- **Unit** (`tests/testutil/`): the predicate returns false for an empty `TMUX_TMPDIR`, false
  for a `TMUX_TMPDIR` that exists but sits outside the `ntm-tmux-test-*` pattern, and true for
  a path produced by `createShortTmuxTempDir()`. Each of the three must be broken on purpose
  and observed to fail before the test is trusted — a guard that cannot fail is not a guard.
- **Unit** (`tests/testutil/`): `IsolateTmuxTestProcess` called with the variable set and a
  bogus `TMUX_TMPDIR` returns a non-nil cleanup and leaves `TMUX_TMPDIR` pointing at a fresh
  isolated root, not at the bogus value.
- **Integration**: one parent test from each of the seven helper re-exec sites, asserting the
  helper child did not create a second temp root under the candidate bases.

## Blast radius

`cmd.Env` lines exactly as they are.

title: Give the repo a worktree tool so br reaches the live tracker from a worktree
description:
## Outcome

The repo owns a worktree tool, and a worktree made with it can run `br` against the live
tracker. Today a contributor or an agent creates one with a raw `git worktree add`, which
materialises tracked files only: `.beads/beads.db` is git-ignored, so it is absent, `br` inside
the worktree silently falls back to the committed `.beads/issues.jsonl` snapshot, and every
tracker read there is stale while every tracker write there is lost or, if committed,
destructive. After this bead there is one documented command that produces a correct worktree,
one that repairs a worktree already made the wrong way, and `AGENTS.md` says which to use.

## Context

**This is measured, not anticipated.** On 2026-08-25 three agents worked three beads in three
worktrees created with raw `git worktree add`. All three hit the same wall independently:

- `br doctor` inside the worktree reported the database missing; one agent worked around it with
  `br --no-db` and read a snapshot frozen at checkout time.
- All three saw their own bead as `assignee: null` and `status: open` although the main tree's
  database had them claimed and `in_progress`. The claim is what keeps a second agent off the
  same work, and inside a worktree it is invisible.
- One agent ran `br update --status in_review`, which wrote into the stale JSONL, and committed
  the result into its pull request. Merging it would have rewritten tracker state for **every**
  bead in the file — including those held by the other agents then running. It was caught in
  review, reverted, and cost that agent a whole extra round.

The failure is silent in both directions, which is what makes it expensive: nothing says the
database is missing except a `br doctor` nobody runs, and a stale read looks exactly like a
correct one.

**What already exists, so this bead does not duplicate it.** `internal/worktrees/` is **product
code** — `WorktreeManager` gives each agent pane its own worktree under
`.ntm/worktrees/<session>/<agent>` at runtime (`internal/worktrees/manager.go:88-105`,
`:235-351`), with `MergeBack`, `RemoveWorktree`, `Cleanup` and a risk-scoring advisor. It is not
contributor tooling and must not be extended into it. Nothing else in the repo calls
`git worktree`: no script under `scripts/`, no `Makefile` target.

**Two mechanisms could fix the tracker half, and picking between them is part of the work.**
Both are real and the evidence for each is cited; the implementer establishes which `br` version
in use actually supports, and says so.

- `.beads/redirect` — `br`'s own designed answer. `.beads/.gitignore:23-25` git-ignores it with
  the comment *"Worktree redirect file (contains relative path to main repo's .beads/) Must not
  be committed as paths would be wrong in other clones"*. That describes exactly this problem.
  Nothing in this repo creates it, `.beads/README.md` does not document it, and it is unknown
  whether `br` writes it itself on `br init` inside a worktree or expects a wrapper to.
- **A symlink into the main tree's `.beads/`** — the mechanism proven in the sibling repo
  `llm-workflow`, whose `bin/worktree` links a per-repo list of git-ignored paths into each new
  worktree with `ln -s` and then verifies each link is genuinely git-ignored before returning.

**The sibling tool is already generic, so this is a port and not a design.** `llm-workflow`'s
`bin/worktree` is 789 lines of bash depending only on `git` and coreutils — no `gh`, no `jq`, no
Python. Its per-repo list of paths to link is read from a `.worktree-links` file at the repo
root, with a hard-coded fallback used only when that file is absent; `.beads` is linked in that
repo because that repo's `.worktree-links` names it, not because the script special-cases a
tracker. Its default branch is detected from `origin/HEAD` with a `main`/`master` probe as
fallback, so `main` needs no code change provided `git remote set-head origin -a` has been run.
It carries two pieces of dead weight for a Go repo: a Cargo build-cache remover keyed to
`/mnt/build`, and guidance text naming a sandbox tool that exists only on one machine.

Its `adopt` subcommand is the half that matters most here, because it repairs a worktree that
was created the wrong way — which is the state all three of today's worktrees were in, and the
state any worktree made by an agent following current `AGENTS.md` will be in.

**`AGENTS.md` currently forbids the flow the repo actually uses.** `AGENTS.md:31-42` states
*"This repository uses exactly one branch: `main`... All work happens on `main`... Do not create
or keep side branches"*. Practice diverged: `agent/<bead-id>` branches are created per unit of
work and merged back through pull requests (`Merge pull request #6 from
gabrielassisxyz/agent/bd-9oo`). An agent that obeys the file works in the main tree; an agent
that follows practice finds no tool and reaches for raw `git worktree add`. Leaving that
contradiction in place would make the new tool undiscoverable, so reconciling it is in scope.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `scripts/worktree.sh new <type>/<desc>` creates a worktree branched from a freshly fetched
      `origin/main` and prints the path to enter. Bash, `set -euo pipefail`, dependencies limited
      to `git` and coreutils — no `gh`, no `jq`, no Python
- [ ] In a worktree it created, `br show <any-bead-id>` reports the same `status` and `assignee`
      as the identical command run in the main tree, for a bead whose state was changed in the
      main tree after the worktree was created. This is the criterion the whole bead exists for:
      check it by changing a bead's status in the main tree and reading it back from the worktree
- [ ] The report states which mechanism was used — `.beads/redirect` or a symlink — and cites the
      evidence that the installed `br` supports it. If `redirect` is used, whether `br` creates it
      itself or the script must write it is answered as an observed fact, not assumed
- [ ] `scripts/worktree.sh adopt <path>` repairs a worktree created by a raw `git worktree add`:
      run it against a deliberately raw worktree and show the same `br show` comparison passing
      afterwards
- [ ] The Cargo build-cache removal and the sandbox-specific guidance text are absent from the
      ported script — a Go repo carries neither
- [ ] `scripts/worktree.sh rm <branch|task>` refuses to remove a worktree holding uncommitted
      changes, unpushed commits, or git-ignored files that exist only there, unless `-f` is given.
      Prove each refusal by triggering it
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` describes the worktree-per-unit-of-work flow and names the tool, replacing the
      "exactly one branch" text that the repo's own history contradicts. It states that the main
      tree stays on `main` as a clean reference
- [ ] `git remote set-head origin -a` is documented as a prerequisite, or the script sets it when
      `origin/HEAD` is missing
- [ ] Done when: a fresh worktree made by the tool, and a raw one repaired by `adopt`, both read
      and write the live tracker, and `AGENTS.md` tells the next agent to use it

## Tests

- **Unit** — the branch-name-to-path slug function, over `feature/x`, `agent/bd-123`, and a name
  containing two slashes. Bash, driven by a small test script under `scripts/`; there is no shell
  test harness in the repo today, so establishing one minimal enough to run from a `Makefile`
  target is part of this.
- **Integration** — the tracker-visibility criterion above, scripted end to end: create a
  worktree, change a bead's status in the main tree, read it back from the worktree, assert
  equality. This is the only test that proves the bead's purpose and it cannot be a unit test.
- **Integration** — `adopt` against a worktree created by a raw `git worktree add`, asserting the
  same equality afterwards.
- **Integration** — each `rm` refusal, driven red on purpose: a dirty worktree, an unpushed
  commit, an ignored-only file. A refusal that cannot be observed failing is not a refusal.

Every test operates on a scratch clone or a temporary worktree, never on the developer's own
tree, and none of them may run `git worktree remove` against a path it did not create.

## Blast radius

New files: `scripts/worktree.sh`, `.worktree-links` (or whatever the chosen mechanism needs), and
one test script. Modified: `AGENTS.md` and a `Makefile` target if the tests need one. **No Go
code is touched** — in particular `internal/worktrees/` is product code for agent panes and stays
untouched. CI runs no shell lint (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:137-169` lints Go only), so a new
bash file is invisible to every existing gate; that is a reason to write the tests, not a reason
to skip them.

## Recovery path

The tool creates and deletes worktrees and branches, so a defect can destroy uncommitted work.
Two constraints follow and both are testable: `rm` never proceeds past its refusals without an
explicit `-f`, and branch deletion uses `git branch -d` and never `-D`, so an unmerged branch is
refused by git itself. Reverting the commit removes the script; worktrees it already created are
ordinary git worktrees and keep working, since the links or redirect file it wrote are inert
data, not a format anything else depends on.
close_reason: Delivered in PR #7 (merged as c0cedbff). scripts/worktree.sh, ported from llm-workflow's bin/worktree without the Cargo cache remover or the machine-specific sandbox text. The tracker mechanism is .beads/redirect, chosen on evidence: br 0.2.22 carries its own error strings for the file, so it implements the mechanism and only needs the file written; a symlink to a live sqlite database from two directory entries was rejected as the sharper edge. new and adopt both write it and then verify br reports 'via redirect from' rather than trusting the write. Adds an unpushed-commit refusal that git worktree remove does not perform on its own, plus scripts/test_worktree.sh (11/11) behind make test-worktree-tool. AGENTS.md now describes the worktree-per-task flow.

title: Two agents in separate worktrees wrote into each other's working trees
description:
## Outcome

Two agents dispatched into two worktrees of the same repository cannot write into each other's
working trees. Either the mechanism that let it happen is found and closed, or the dispatch path
detects it and refuses, so an orchestrator never merges a branch whose tree was edited by a
process it did not send there.

## Steps to Reproduce

Observed, not constructed — the mechanism is the open question and finding it is most of this
bead's work.

1. Dispatch two agents at the same time into two worktrees of one repository, each on its own
   branch. Measured with `ntm`, worktrees `bugfix-give-the-last-fixed-tmux-session-name-a`
   (bead `bd-pl0`) and `feature-give-robot-rano-stats-a-session-filter` (bead `bd-y5rmg`), each
   created by `scripts/worktree.sh new`, each driven by its own `pi` process.
2. Let both run to completion. Both committed the correct change to their own branch.
3. `git status` in each worktree afterwards:
   - `bd-pl0`'s tree held **seven uncommitted files belonging to `bd-y5rmg`** —
     `internal/robot/rano_stats.go`, `internal/cli/robot_session_flag_test.go`,
     `internal/cli/rotate.go` and others.
   - `bd-y5rmg`'s tree held **eight uncommitted files belonging to `bd-pl0`**, byte-identical to
     that branch's commit `21e7ecd8`.

The two diffs were compared mechanically. `bd-pl0`'s work appearing in `bd-y5rmg`'s tree is
identical to its commit. `bd-y5rmg`'s work appearing in `bd-pl0`'s tree is its commit plus one
stray line, `fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "DEBUG-ROTATE: path=%s args=%v\n", ...)`, which the agent
left behind and never committed.

## Context

Measured 2026-08-26 during an unattended run that dispatched roughly thirty beads across four
repositories. These were the only two lanes where it happened, and they were also the two longest
runs of the day — 57 minutes, 421 and 500 turns — and the two doing the most work outside a single
file: `bd-pl0` sweeping every test file for literal tmux session names, `bd-y5rmg` spawning live
tmux sessions to probe robot flag state.

**The main working tree was clean throughout**, so this is not "an agent edited the shared
checkout". Each pair of edits crossed directly from one worktree into the other.

**Why this matters more than the mess it left.** The orchestrator caught it only because it runs
`git status` before merging. Nothing else would have: both branches' commits were correct, both
gates were green, and both pull requests were clean. Had either agent committed with `git commit
-a` or staged by directory, it would have carried the other bead's half-finished work into its
own pull request under its own bead id, and the reviewer would have had no signal at all. The
`DEBUG-ROTATE` line is the proof that at least one of the crossed sets was *not* finished work.

**What is not yet known, and is the first job here:** the mechanism. Candidates worth ruling in
or out before writing any fix — a sweep whose glob or `sed` invocation escaped its worktree via a
relative path with `..`; a tool run with an absolute path from a previous `cd`; a test helper
that resolves a repository root by walking upwards and finds the wrong one; a shared temporary or
cache directory that one process wrote through. `scripts/worktree.sh` writes `.beads/redirect`
into each worktree deliberately, which is a real cross-worktree path, but it points at the
tracker rather than at source, so it explains nothing here on its own.

Do not fix a candidate without first reproducing the crossing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The mechanism is identified and stated with the evidence that identified it — a command
      line, a resolved path, or a reproduction. "Probably a glob" is not an answer.
- [ ] The crossing is reproduced deliberately at least once, so the fix has something to be
      tested against.
- [ ] Whatever allowed it is closed, or if it cannot be closed, the dispatch path gains a check
      that compares a worktree's dirty file set against the bead's blast radius and refuses to
      merge on a mismatch.
- [ ] A test covers the reproduction, and fails when the fix is reverted.
- [ ] If the mechanism turns out to be a repository tool rather than the agent, that tool's own
      documentation says so, since every future dispatch inherits it.
- [ ] Done when: two agents driven concurrently in two worktrees of this repository leave each
      other's trees untouched, checked by `git status` in both after they finish.

## Tests

- **Integration (shell), the deliverable:** drive two concurrent processes doing broad file
  sweeps in two worktrees of one repository, then assert each tree's dirty set is a subset of the
  files that process was told to touch.
- **Unit:** whatever path-resolution helper turns out to be at fault gets a case pinning it to
  the worktree it was called from.
- **Mutation, before either is trusted:** revert the fix and confirm the integration test goes
  red. A test that passes both ways proves nothing here, and this defect was invisible to every
  gate that already exists.

## Blast radius

Unknown until the mechanism is found, which is itself the reason this bead exists rather than a
patch. Expected to be small — one path resolution, or one check added to the dispatch path. If
the investigation shows it is wide, stop and say so rather than widening the change.

## Recovery path

Nothing migrates and no data is rewritten. The leftovers found on 2026-08-26 were **stashed, not
discarded**, in both worktrees; those worktrees have since been removed, so the stashes went with
them, and the commits they duplicated are on `main`.
close_reason: verified at d48fb812. Mechanism found and independently reproduced by the orchestrator, not taken on the agent's word: git's stash stack is one per REPOSITORY, living in the common git dir's refs/stash, not one per worktree. Two worktrees that stash and pop interleaved each restore the other's changes. Reproduced from scratch in a fresh two-worktree repo: after A stashes, B stashes, A pops, B pops, wt-a holds b.txt and wt-b holds a.txt - the exact crossing seen on bd-pl0 and bd-y5rmg, whose pi transcripts show both stashes landing within 8 seconds of each other and both pops after. Mutation independently re-run: changing the check's set difference (comm -23) to an intersection (comm -12) turns the crossed-worktree case red with 'the check is blind to the crossing'. make build green, contamination suite 4/4, the existing worktree suite still 11/11. make lint is red identically on main. PR #31 merged.

title: Tests write into the real config directory: isolation covers tmux and git but not os.UserConfigDir
description:
## Outcome

Running the test suite does not write into the config directory of whoever runs it. Tests that
persist Agent Mail identities, session registries or any other `os.UserConfigDir()`-derived state
write to a per-process temporary root, so a developer's `~/.config/ntm/sessions/` is unchanged
after a run. The isolation is process-wide, in the same place tmux isolation already lives, rather
than being remembered test by test.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Note what is in the real config directory: `ls ~/.config/ntm/sessions/`.
2. Run a package that exercises Agent Mail identity persistence, with no `-short`:
   `go test ./internal/coordinator/ -run TestUpdateAgentStatesLoadsPersistedAgentMailIdentity -count=1`.
3. List the directory again. It now holds a session directory named after the test's own Go
   temporary directory, containing an `agent_registry.json`.

Measured 2026-08-24 on `v1.26.0-36-gfd827f46`. Three such directories were left behind by three
separate runs, at 18:04, 18:08 and 18:10:

    ~/.config/ntm/sessions/registry-identity-session/
      mnt-build-go-tmp-testupdateagentstatesloadspersistedagentmailidentity3072845671-002/agent_registry.json
      mnt-build-go-tmp-testupdateagentstatesloadspersistedagentmailidentity3220743508-002/agent_registry.json
      mnt-build-go-tmp-testupdateagentstatesloadspersistedagentmailidentity1059596228-002/agent_registry.json

## Context

The suite already has process-wide isolation for the two resources it was known to damage, and the
config directory is not one of them. `testutil.IsolateTmuxTestProcess`
(`tests/testutil/throttle.go:161-188`) sets `TMUX`, `TMUX_PANE` and `TMUX_TMPDIR`, and
`testutil.IsolateGitConfigProcess` covers git. Neither touches `HOME` or `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, so
anything resolving a path through `os.UserConfigDir()` still lands in the real home.

`internal/agentmail/session.go:43` is that resolver: the session directory is built from
`os.UserConfigDir()`, which reads `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and falls back to `$HOME/.config`. A test that
registers an agent therefore writes a real session directory under the developer's config.

The exposure is uneven across packages, which is why this looks like an isolated incident rather
than a systematic gap. `internal/cli` (`internal/cli/testmain_test.go:35-60`), `internal/robot`
(`internal/robot/robot_test.go:152`) and `internal/status` each call `IsolateTmuxTestProcess` from
`TestMain`; `internal/coordinator`, where the test above lives, calls no isolation helper at all.
So the same defect is one `TestMain` away in every package that has not needed tmux.

**Two further leaks were observed in the same window and are reported here as evidence rather than
as this bead's target**, because their cause is different — a cleanup that does not run rather than
a missing environment override:

- 1221 leftover `/var/tmp/ntm-tmux-test-*` directories. The root is created by
  `createShortTmuxTempDir` and removed only by the cleanup closure
  (`tests/testutil/throttle.go:192-210`), so every test process that is killed rather than exiting
  leaves its root behind.
- A `tmux new-session -d -s quick-fallback` client from
  `TestRunQuickUsesDefaultProjectsBaseWhenConfigNil` left hung in state `Ss` for over 27 minutes
  after its test binary was gone.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After `go test ./internal/coordinator/ -count=1` with no `-short`, `~/.config/ntm/sessions/`
      contains exactly what it contained before the run — asserted by comparing a listing taken
      before and after, not by inspection
- [ ] The isolation is applied process-wide from `TestMain`, in the same helper family as
      `IsolateTmuxTestProcess` and `IsolateGitConfigProcess`, rather than per test
- [ ] The helper overrides both `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `HOME`, since `os.UserConfigDir()` falls back
      to `$HOME/.config` when the former is unset
- [ ] Every package whose tests can reach `os.UserConfigDir()` calls it — the audit that establishes
      which packages those are is part of the work, and its result is recorded in the commit body
- [ ] A test that deliberately asserts on the isolated config path still passes, so the override is
      readable by the code under test and not merely blocked
- [ ] The tmux and git isolation already in place is unchanged
- [ ] Done when: a full-suite run on a machine with a populated `~/.config/ntm/` leaves that
      directory byte-identical, verified by a checksum of the tree taken before and after.

## Tests

- **Unit test** — the new helper: with it active, `os.UserConfigDir()` resolves under the temporary
  root and not under the caller's real home. Assert on the resolved path, not on the env var.
- **Unit test** — the helper's cleanup restores the previous values, including the case where
  `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` was unset before the call, which must be restored to unset rather than to empty.
- **Regression test** — `TestUpdateAgentStatesLoadsPersistedAgentMailIdentity` writes its registry
  under the isolated root: assert the file exists at the isolated path, which fails if the override
  is not reaching `internal/agentmail`.
- **Guard test** — a test that fails if a package known to touch the config dir has a `TestMain`
  without the helper, so the audit does not decay the first time a package is added.

Every assertion must be driven red on purpose: a test that passes against the current code is not
testing this bead.

## Blast radius

`tests/testutil/` for the new helper, and the `TestMain` of each package the audit names —
`internal/coordinator` at minimum. Production code is not changed:
`internal/agentmail/session.go:43` keeps resolving through `os.UserConfigDir()`, which is correct
behaviour that the tests were failing to contain.

## Recovery path

Test-harness only, with no production behaviour and no persisted state, so reverting the commit
restores the previous behaviour exactly. Directories already written into a real config directory
by earlier runs are not migrated or deleted by this change; they are removed by hand, as they were
on 2026-08-24.
close_reason: Implemented in 0414f78c, with a follow-up in 6f12cac7. IsolateUserConfigProcess overrides XDG_CONFIG_HOME and HOME to a private temp root and restores an unset variable to unset; called from TestMain in e2e, agentmail, cli, coordinator, robot and tests/e2e. Proven by the operator, not asserted: sha256 of the real ~/.config/ntm tree is identical before and after 'go test ./internal/coordinator/ -count=1' run with NO override, the exact command that polluted it three times on 2026-08-24. The agent found a consequence the bead missed: redirecting HOME also redirects Go's module cache, whose read-only files defeat a bare os.RemoveAll, hence removeAllWritable. The guard test as first written could not fail - it tracked 'has TestMain' and 'mentions the helper' independently across the package, so a comment satisfied it; tightened to require both in the same file and a call rather than a mention, and proven red by replacing one TestMain's call.

title: bv not found reports 'not installed' when it is merely off PATH
description:
## Outcome

When `bv` cannot be found, the error says which condition actually holds and names the `PATH` it
searched, instead of telling the operator to install something that is already installed.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Arrange for `bv` to be installed somewhere not on the `PATH` of the calling process. On the
   machine where this was hit, `bv` lives at `/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin/bv`, which the systemd
   user manager's default `PATH` does not include.
2. Run an assignment that reaches the actionable-work check from that process.
3. The failure reads
   `actionable bv plan could not be verified: load bv --robot-triage: bv is not installed`, with the
   install instruction `go install github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer@latest`.

`bv` is installed. The condition named is wrong and the remedy offered does not apply. Recorded 19
times in one dispatch ledger.

## Context

Hit while driving an unattended swarm on 2026-08-27, from a systemd user unit.

The failure is latent, which is what made it expensive: the code path is only reached once a bead
actually becomes dispatchable, so nine ticks exited zero before the tenth failed. An operator reading
the journal sees a clean run and then a message telling them to install something that is already
there, which sends them to the wrong machine state entirely.

**Where the code is, corrected after review.** An earlier version of this bead named
`internal/bv/triage.go:28`. That file only defines the wrapping sentinel
`ErrActionablePlanUnverified`. The parts that matter are:

- `internal/bv/bv.go:31` — `var ErrNotInstalled = errors.New("bv is not installed")`
- `internal/bv/client.go:368` — where the user-facing message and the `go install` instruction are
  built onto that sentinel
- `internal/bv/bv.go:104` — the lookup, a bare `exec.LookPath("bv")`

**And the distinction to draw is not the obvious one.** The first version of this bead asked for
"not installed" to be told apart from "installed but not on `PATH`". `exec.LookPath` cannot answer
that: it searches `PATH` and nothing else, so `exec.ErrNotFound` means *not found on this `PATH`* and
carries no information about whether the binary exists elsewhere on the filesystem. Asking for that
distinction would send an implementer looking for a signal that is not there, or worse, to a
filesystem scan.

What `LookPath` does distinguish, and what is genuinely useful, is *not found on `PATH`* against
*found but not executable* — `ErrNotFound` against a permission error. Combined with printing the
`PATH` that was searched, that is enough for the operator to tell the two real situations apart
without the program having to guess.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When the lookup fails, the message names the `PATH` that was searched. That single addition is
      what turns this from a wrong diagnosis into a correct one, since an operator who can see the
      `PATH` can see that their install directory is missing from it.
- [ ] `exec.ErrNotFound` and a permission error produce different messages: not found on this `PATH`,
      against found but not executable.
- [ ] The `go install` instruction is not presented as the remedy for a `PATH` problem. Either it
      moves behind the genuinely-absent branch, or it is reworded so it does not read as the only
      cause.
- [ ] The message does not claim to know whether `bv` exists elsewhere on the filesystem, because the
      lookup cannot know that.
- [ ] Both branches are reachable from a test and the test distinguishes them.
- [ ] Done when: the message names the condition that actually holds.

## Tests

Unit tests around the lookup in `internal/bv/bv.go`: one with a `PATH` that excludes a real binary,
asserting the not-on-`PATH` branch and that the searched `PATH` appears in the message; one with the
binary present but not executable, asserting the other branch.

The existing assertions at `e2e/robot_bulk_assign_test.go:806` and `e2e/robot_format_test.go:3164`
match on the current string and will need updating in step with it.

## Blast radius

`internal/bv/bv.go` (the lookup and the sentinel) and `internal/bv/client.go` (the message), plus the
two e2e tests that assert on the current text. `internal/bv/triage.go` is not touched; it only wraps.
No behaviour changes beyond the error text and which branch produces it, so nothing that succeeds
today begins failing.
close_reason: Merged in PR #35. The lookup now names the condition and the searched PATH; ErrNotOnPATH and ErrNotExecutable wrap ErrNotInstalled so errors.Is callers are unchanged. Correction to the bead's Context: exec.LookPath cannot distinguish the two on unix — Go discards every per-candidate error and returns ErrNotFound unconditionally (findExecutable in os/exec/lp_unix.go, verified against Go 1.26.5), so the distinction is recovered by re-walking the same PATH entries after the lookup fails. Not touched, same defect, own change: internal/context/pack.go, internal/tools/bv.go, internal/tui/dashboard/*.

title: Decide how a consumer joins a pane's session id to its transcript file
description:
## Outcome

A decision is recorded on how a consumer gets from a pane's agent CLI session id to the transcript
file on disk, and the next person who needs that join executes it instead of re-opening the argument.

## Context

`bd-4gw` put `agent_session_id` on `--robot-is-working --session-id`: each pane now reports the
session id of the CLI running in it. That is the middle edge of `bead -> pane -> transcript`. The
last edge — id to file — is not published anywhere.

`bd-f4a` set out to close it with an exported resolver and could not. The resolver was written and
worked; `scripts/guards/deadcode_gate.sh` rejected it with
`internal/agentsession/discover.go:TranscriptPath` unreachable from `cmd/ntm`, because no production
code calls it. That is the repository's One Reachable Implementation rule doing its job — "any PR
that lands an engine must, in the same PR, land the user surface" — not a gate misfiring. The
consolidation half of `bd-f4a` shipped (PR #10); the resolver half did not.

Three facts constrain every option below.

**The shape of the resolver is settled and does not need rediscovering.** It is answerable from an id
plus a working directory for exactly two providers: Claude
(`<home>/.claude/projects/<ClaudeProjectDir(cwd)>/<id>.jsonl`) and Antigravity
(`<home>/.gemini/antigravity-cli/conversations/<id>.db`). It is not answerable for Codex, which
shards rollouts by date and identifies them by a cwd embedded in the file body
(`internal/agentsession/discover.go:1014-1053`), nor for Gemini, which resolves its chat directory
through a `projects.json` registry with a `sha256(cwd)` fallback (`discover.go:1129-1132`,
`:1176-1204`). For those two, scanning is the only answer.

**A Go caller inside this repository already has the join and needs nothing.**
`Discoverer.DiscoverContext` returns an `Info` whose `SourcePath` is the file discovery actually
found, for all four providers. The field is exported Go; only `json:"-"` withholds it from
serialization. So this decision is about consumers OUTSIDE the process, not about ntm's own code.

**Publishing the path in JSON was refused once, with a reason.**
`internal/agentsession/discover.go:90` states that `SourcePath` stays process-private "so status
surfaces do not expose local transcript locations". Any option that emits a path in robot output
re-opens that decision rather than working around it.

The consumer that motivated all of this is the token-spend attribution tool named in `bd-4gw`: it
wants to attribute spend to a bead and its stated rule is that a number it cannot justify is not
printed. Today it must correlate on timestamps, or reimplement each provider's layout — which is the
duplication `bd-f4a` just deleted from this repository.

## Options

- **A · Wait for the consumer.** Nothing lands until something needs it; the resolver arrives in the
  same PR as its first caller. What changes: the tree stays free of unreachable code and the gate
  stays honest, at the cost that whoever needs the join next writes the resolver themselves. That
  cost is small and bounded — its shape is in the Context above and in `bd-f4a`'s comments — but it
  is paid by a future session, possibly under time pressure, and the risk is that they reimplement
  the layout inline instead, which is exactly the defect just removed.
- **B · Waive it now.** Land the resolver plus its unit tests behind a line in
  `ci/allowlists/deadcode.txt` (`<entry>\t<bead-id>\t<reason>`, which the protocol permits with an
  open bead). What changes: the code and its tests exist and are exercised in CI, so a provider
  layout change is caught by a test rather than by a consumer getting a path to nothing; the cost is
  one more entry in a 2,037-line debt ledger, deliberately added rather than inherited, and code
  whose only exercise is its own test — which is how a function drifts from what callers would
  actually want from it.
- **C · Build the surface now.** Land the resolver together with a user surface that returns the
  path, so it is reachable by the rule's own terms — either a new field under the existing
  `--session-id` opt-in, or a separate robot verb. What changes: non-Go consumers get the join
  immediately and the gate is satisfied without a waiver; the cost is that robot output starts
  carrying local filesystem paths, which reverses the decision recorded at `discover.go:90`, and it
  is the only option here that has to be argued on privacy grounds rather than on engineering ones.
  It also answers for only two of the four providers, so the surface must express "not answerable"
  without a consumer mistaking it for "no session".

## What decides it

**How the attribution consumer talks to ntm.** If it links Go, it already has `Info.SourcePath` for
all four providers and needs none of this — A is free and B and C are work for nobody. If it shells
out to `ntm --robot-*` and parses JSON, then only C ever gives it the join, and A merely postpones C
while B never reaches it. That question is answerable today by looking at how the consumer is built,
and it should be answered before this bead is closed.

Second, and only if the answer is "it shells out": whether a local transcript path in robot JSON is
acceptable on this machine, given that the reason it was withheld was exposure through status
surfaces rather than a security boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One of A, B or C is chosen and written on this bead, with the reason, not just the letter
- [ ] The choice names how the attribution consumer reaches ntm (Go import or CLI), since that is
      what decides it
- [ ] If C is chosen, the decision explicitly says whether `discover.go:90`'s process-private rule is
      amended or scoped, so the next reader does not find two rules that contradict each other
- [ ] The follow-on work exists as a bead when the choice implies work (B and C do; A does not)
- [ ] Done when: this bead is closed carrying the decision, and `internal/agentsession`'s comments
      agree with whatever was decided

## Recovery path

A decision with no code. Reversing it means writing a different one here; nothing is deployed,
migrated or serialized by closing this bead.

title: Export the transcript-path resolver so nothing reimplements a provider's session layout
description:
## Outcome

The rule that turns a provider session id into an on-disk transcript path exists in exactly one
place per provider, and it is reachable by name from outside `internal/agentsession`. Nothing in
this repository reimplements a provider's directory layout in order to find a transcript, and the
in-process contract for a Go caller that needs the path is stated where the field is declared
rather than inferred from a JSON tag.

## Context

`bd-4gw` added `agent_session_id` to `--robot-is-working --session-id`: each pane now reports the
session id of the agent CLI running in it, which is the middle edge of `bead -> pane -> transcript`.
The id alone is only half of a join. Getting from the id to the file means knowing the provider's
own layout, and that knowledge is currently private to `internal/agentsession`.

The evidence that this costs something is already in the tree. `internal/robot/is_working_session_id_test.go:24`
declares `claudeProjectDirEncodingForTest`, a copy of the production regexp `claudeNonAlnumPattern`
(`internal/agentsession/discover.go:38`), and reimplements `encodeClaudeProjectDir`
(`discover.go:845-848`) inline at lines 58 and 132. The test's own comment says why: the production
encoder is unexported. A test inside the repo had to duplicate production logic to locate a file the
production code had just located, and a duplicated encoding is one that silently goes stale when the
provider changes its layout — a wrong path returns "no such file", not "your copy is out of date".

**What is genuinely reconstructable, and what is not.** These differ per provider and the difference
decides the shape of the fix:

| provider | how the path is reached today |
| --- | --- |
| Claude (`cc`) | pure function of the working directory: `<home>/.claude/projects/<encodeClaudeProjectDir(workDir)>/<id>.jsonl` (`discover.go:856-876`). No I/O, no scan |
| Antigravity (`agy`) | flat join `<home>/.gemini/antigravity-cli/conversations/<id>.db`, but only ever written inline inside the scan (`discover.go:1301`) |
| Codex (`cod`) | no formula at all — a `filepath.WalkDir` over a date-sharded tree filtering on the cwd embedded in each rollout file (`discover.go:1014-1053`) |
| Gemini (`gmi`) | needs `projects.json` I/O, or a `sha256(workDir)` legacy fallback (`discover.go:1129-1132`, `:1176-1204`) |

So "given an id, compute the path" is answerable without scanning for Claude and Antigravity, and
is not answerable for Codex and Gemini. A resolver that pretended otherwise would be a function that
lies for half its inputs.

**Publishing the path in JSON is not the fix, and that is settled.** `Info.SourcePath`
(`discover.go:82`) and `BindingObservation.SourcePath` (`discover.go:102`) are `json:"-"` with the
reason written at `discover.go:90`: *"SourcePath remains process-private so status surfaces do not
expose local transcript locations"*. That fence stands. What this bead changes is only what an
in-repo Go caller can name — both fields are already exported Go fields that any package here can
read, which nothing states outside that one comment.

A non-Go consumer still cannot walk the join after this bead. That is deliberate: giving it one
means a new CLI or robot surface, which is its own bead and its own surface decision, not a
side effect of a refactor.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The Claude project-directory encoding is exported from `internal/agentsession` under a name
      that says what it produces, and `discoverClaudeContext` calls the exported name, so the
      exported symbol is reachable from `cmd/ntm` and the dead-code gate passes unchanged
- [ ] A caller holding a provider, a session id and a working directory can obtain a transcript path
      through an exported function for the providers where that is answerable without scanning
      (Claude, Antigravity), and receives an explicit not-answerable result for Codex and Gemini
      rather than a constructed path that may not exist
- [ ] `internal/robot/is_working_session_id_test.go` no longer declares its own copy of the
      encoding: `claudeProjectDirEncodingForTest` is deleted and the test calls the exported
      function. `command grep -rn 'a-zA-Z0-9' internal/robot` returns no path-encoding regexp
- [ ] The doc comment on the exported resolver states which providers are pure and which require
      discovery, so a caller does not have to read `discover.go` to learn that a nil result for
      Codex is the contract rather than a bug
- [ ] `SourcePath`'s existing comment is extended to say that in-process Go callers may read the
      field and only JSON serialization is withheld, so the fence is not mistaken for "unreachable"
- [ ] No JSON output anywhere in the repo gains a filesystem path: `git diff` shows no new
      `json:"..."` tag on any `SourcePath`, and `--robot-is-working --session-id` output is
      byte-identical to before this bead for the same input
- [ ] Done when: the robot test locates its planted transcript through the exported resolver, with
      no encoding logic of its own, and `go build ./cmd/ntm` plus `scripts/guards/deadcode_gate.sh`
      are green

## Tests

- **Unit (Go, `internal/agentsession`):** the exported encoder returns the same string as the
  layout `discoverClaudeContext` builds, for a working directory containing every character class
  that gets rewritten (spaces, dots, slashes, accented bytes). Table-driven, asserted against
  literal expected strings rather than against the regexp itself, so a change to the pattern fails
  the test instead of being mirrored by it
- **Unit (Go, `internal/agentsession`):** the resolver returns a path for Claude and Antigravity and
  an explicit not-answerable result for Codex and Gemini, one case per provider. This is the test
  that fails if someone later "completes" the resolver by constructing a Codex path that does not
  exist
- **Unit (Go, `internal/robot`):** the existing `TestGetIsWorkingReportsAgentSessionIDMatchingRealTranscriptFile`
  keeps passing with its local encoder deleted and the exported resolver in its place — the
  regression check that the exported behaviour matches what the test was hand-rolling

## Blast radius

`internal/agentsession/discover.go` (rename one unexported function to its exported form, add one
resolver and its doc comment, extend one field comment) plus its new unit tests, and
`internal/robot/is_working_session_id_test.go` (delete the duplicate encoder, call the resolver).
No production behaviour changes: no new JSON field, no new flag, no change to what
`--robot-is-working` emits, and no change to how discovery scans.

## Recovery path

Pure refactor plus additive exported symbols. Reverting the commit restores the unexported encoder
and the test's local copy; no state, no schema and no serialized output is touched, so nothing
persisted needs undoing.

title: Discover pi session ids so the largest agent lane reaches the transcript join
description:
## Outcome

A `pi` pane reports its agent CLI session id on `--robot-is-working --session-id`, resolving to the
transcript that pane actually wrote, and two `pi` panes running in the same working directory report
two different ids. The lane that carries most of this machine's agent turns stops being the one lane
the bead-to-transcript join cannot reach.

## Context

`bd-4gw` shipped `agent_session_id`. Measured on 2026-08-26 against the live `agent-usage-book`
swarm: 7 panes, and exactly 1 carried the field. The other 6 are `pi`, and they are silent for a
reason that is correct in the code and wrong for the goal — `ResumeProvider`
(`internal/agentsession/discover.go:120-133`) recognizes only `cc`, `cod`, `gmi` and `agy`, so
`DiscoverContext` returns nil at `:203-205` before any discovery runs. No error, no log, no field.
The one pane that answered was `cc`, and its id resolved end to end:
`~/.claude/projects/-home-gabriel-repositories-agent-usage-book/0bb02dc5-….jsonl`, 387 KB, mtime
tracking the live session.

**`pi` has a transcript store, and its layout is as derivable as Claude's.** Sessions live at
`~/.pi/agent/sessions/<encoded-cwd>/<ISO-timestamp>_<uuid>.jsonl`, where the directory is the working
directory with every `/` replaced by `-` and the whole wrapped in `--` (measured:
`/home/gabriel/repositories/agent-usage-book` → `--home-gabriel-repositories-agent-usage-book--`).
The first line of each file is a header record whose keys are `type`, `version`, `id`, `timestamp`,
`cwd` — so the session id is readable from the file itself and the cwd is verifiable, exactly the
structured shape `discoverCodexContext` relies on for Codex, without Codex's date sharding.

**The hard part is not the layout, it is which of several files belongs to which pane, and the
mechanism this package already uses does not work for `pi`.** Existing per-pane disambiguation walks
the pane's own process tree and reads open file handles: `discoverProcessSession`
(`discover.go:597-628`) → `processNodeSession` (`:630-653`) → `openSessionFiles` (`:700-714`, reading
`/proc/<pid>/fd`) → `isProviderSessionFile` (`:779-797`). Measured on a live `pi` process (pid 54109,
`pi --approve --model deepseek-v4-pro-high-k1`): its open descriptors are the pty, `/dev/urandom`,
eventfd/timerfd and `/proc/self/statm` — **no descriptor on its own session file**. `pi` appends and
closes, so the open-fd scan finds nothing and returns no session however correctly `pi` is added to
`providerCommandMarkers`. That is the trap this bead exists to state: the obvious three-line
"register another provider" change compiles, passes a single-pane test, and silently reports nothing
whenever more than one `pi` runs in a directory.

**Time is the remaining signal, and naive time matching is measurably wrong.** The six live panes,
process start (from `/proc/<pid>/stat`, the same source as `agentProcessStartMillis`,
`discover.go:557-590`) against the session header each one wrote:

| pane pid | process start | header written | lag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 54109 | 02:46:52.460 | 02:46:53.012 | 552 ms |
| 54217 | 02:46:52.580 | 02:46:53.174 | 594 ms |
| 54384 | 02:46:52.700 | 02:46:53.330 | 630 ms |
| 54509 | 02:46:52.810 | 02:46:53.563 | 753 ms |
| 54691 | 02:46:52.930 | 02:46:53.692 | 762 ms |
| 54851 | 02:46:53.070 | 02:46:53.851 | 781 ms |

Consecutive panes start 110-140 ms apart while the write lag is 552-781 ms, so **the lag exceeds the
spacing by a factor of about five**. Nearest-header-by-time assigns the first header to five of the
six panes — measured, not predicted. What does work is ordered assignment: the i-th process by start
time takes the i-th unclaimed header after it, which was exact for all six. That requires two things
a per-pane function does not have on its own — the set of panes considered together, and a record of
what has already been taken. Both already exist: `GetIsWorking` builds ONE `Discoverer` for the whole
call (`internal/robot/is_working.go`), and that `Discoverer` already carries `claimedSessions` with
`markClaimed`/`isClaimed` (`discover.go:354-360`) for exactly this purpose on other providers.

**What a fifth provider touches**, so the work is not discovered halfway through: a `pi` arm in
`ResumeProvider` (`discover.go:120-133`), a `discoverPiContext` plus its case in the native-fallback
switch (`:284-293`), a case in `canonicalAgentType` (`:502-515`), an entry in
`providerCommandMarkers` (`:529-538`) so the process tree recognizes a `pi` child, and the three
provider switches in `resume.go` (`:40-47`, `:53-65`, `:75-79`). CASR is gated to Codex and Gemini
(`:265-267`) and stays that way — nothing suggests casr knows `pi`. Nothing in `internal/agent`
changes: `AgentTypePi` (`internal/agent/types.go:20`) and its parser patterns already exist, which is
why the pane is correctly typed `pi` in the output above while carrying no session.

**Adjacent and deliberately out of scope:** `internal/session/capture.go:182-211` (`countAgents`) and
`internal/session/restore.go:561-587` (`getAgentCommand`) switch over every agent type and have no
`tmux.AgentPi` case, so a `pi` pane is uncounted in `AgentConfig.Total()` and has no default launch
command. That gap predates this bead and is not created by it. Flagged, not fixed here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ResumeProvider("pi")` returns a non-empty provider, and `--robot-is-working --session-id`
      reports `agent_session_id` for a `pi` pane whose transcript exists
- [ ] The reported id names a file that exists under `~/.pi/agent/sessions/<encoded-cwd>/`, verified
      by stat'ing the path built from the reported id rather than from the planted fixture
- [ ] Six `pi` panes started within one second in the same working directory report six DISTINCT
      ids, each matching the header its own process wrote. This is the criterion the naive
      implementation fails: nearest-by-time collides on the first header for five of six
- [ ] A session already assigned to one pane is never reported for a second pane in the same call,
      using the existing `claimedSessions` record rather than a new mechanism
- [ ] A `pi` pane whose transcript cannot be identified reports no `agent_session_id` at all, rather
      than the newest file in the directory. A wrong id is worse than an absent one, because the
      consumer joins on it
- [ ] `--session-id` remains opt-in and the default `--robot-is-working` path performs no `~/.pi`
      filesystem access, matching the flag's existing contract
- [ ] Done when: the live seven-pane swarm shape (six `pi`, one `cc`) reports seven ids, and each one
      resolves to a distinct file on disk

## Tests

- **Unit (Go, `internal/agentsession`):** `TestDiscoverPi`, following the fixture pattern of
  `TestDiscoverClaude` (`agentsession_test.go:423-466`) — temp `HOME`, planted
  `~/.pi/agent/sessions/<encoded-cwd>/<ts>_<uuid>.jsonl` with a real header line, asserting
  `SessionID`, `Provider` and `SourcePath`
- **Unit (Go):** the directory encoding round-trips a cwd with characters that get rewritten, asserted
  against literal expected strings rather than against the encoder's own expression
- **Unit (Go):** a header whose `cwd` does not match the requested working directory is rejected
  rather than returned, so a stale directory cannot answer for another project
- **Unit (Go), the one that matters:** six planted sessions and six simulated process start times
  reproducing the measured spacing (120 ms apart, headers 550-780 ms later) must yield six distinct
  assignments. Written so that a nearest-by-time implementation fails it — that implementation is the
  one a reader reaches for first
- **Unit (Go):** `TestResumeProvider` (`agentsession_test.go:46-76`) gains its `pi` row, and
  `TestDiscoverNonResumableAgent` (`:468-476`) is checked for a stale premise, since `pi` moves out of
  the non-resumable bucket
- **Integration (Go, `internal/robot`):** the `--session-id` opt-in test grows a `pi` pane alongside
  the existing `cc` one, proving both providers answer in one call and that the opt-out path still
  touches no provider directory

## Blast radius

`internal/agentsession/discover.go` (one new discover function plus arms in four existing switches),
`internal/agentsession/resume.go` (three provider switches), their tests, and the existing
`--session-id` test in `internal/robot`. No change to the robot output schema — the field already
exists — no new flag, no change to what the default poll path does, and no change to how the four
current providers are discovered.

## Recovery path

Additive: a provider that did not resolve before starts resolving. Reverting the commit returns
`ResumeProvider("pi")` to `""`, which is exactly today's behaviour — the field goes absent again for
`pi` panes and nothing else changes. No stored state, no schema, no serialized output is touched.

title: Deliver spawn prompts to pi panes: readiness resolves state=unknown at 0.25
description:
## Outcome

`ntm spawn` delivers prompts to `pi` panes. A six-pane pi swarm launches with every prompt
delivered, instead of every pane failing `user_prompt readiness ... timeout ... last
state=unknown freshness=fresh confidence=0.25` while sitting at a healthy pi prompt. The
readiness poll — not only the classifier layer under it — is covered by a test for a
non-`cc`/`cod` agent type, so the next classifier that lands is known to reach the gate that
uses it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install ntm at `d58a18eb` or later (`bin/binary-drift` clean; `ntm --version` reports
   `v1.26.0-16-gd58a18eb`). This is the commit that merged PR #3 and therefore already
   carries `0a771c3a`, "give pi a readiness classifier".
2. `ntm spawn` a six-pane session with agent type `pi`.
3. Every pane comes up at a working pi prompt.
4. Spawn fails all six:

```
spawn prompt setup failed: pane %252: agent 1 (pi): user_prompt readiness for pane %252:
timeout waiting for pane %252 to become ready; last state=unknown freshness=fresh
confidence=0.25; pane %253: agent 2 (pi): ... (and so on for all six)
```

No prompt is delivered to any pane. Recovery is manual delivery to six panes.

Observed three times on that binary, on separate days: 2026-08-22 15:20, 2026-08-23 17:57 and
2026-08-23 21:20, six panes each, 18 of 18 panes, identical signature every time. Recorded in
the kernl-da run ledger (`~/.local/state/kernl-da/runs.jsonl`, `bin/run-log friction`), where
`ntm` is the largest non-`Bash` friction bucket of the window — 17 rows across 13 of 33 runs,
10 of them readiness or delivery.

## Context

**This is not the stale-binary case, and it is not the case bd-zz717 covers.** Two nearby
explanations are already ruled out:

- The 2026-08-22 12:15 session replaced the installed binary (its backup is named
  `ntm.pre-pi-readiness-v1.24.0-3-g28bd96c9`), so the three reproductions above ran on the
  commit that added pi classification, not before it.
- `bd-zz717` makes the readiness verdict *visible* per pane at spawn. Visibility is worth
  having and would have shortened the diagnosis, but a verdict line does not deliver a prompt.
  This bead is the delivery failing; that one is nobody being told.

**Where the failure sits, traced but not closed.** The timeout string is built by
`spawnReadinessError` off `waitForSpawnPaneReady` (`internal/cli/spawn.go`), which polls every
`spawnReadyPollInterval` (200ms) until `spawnPromptReadyTimeout` (30s). Readiness needs
`spawnPaneObservationSafeToDispatch`, which requires both `pane.SafeToDispatch()` and an
independent re-parse through `agent.NewParser().ParseWithHint`. `SafeToDispatch`
(`internal/status/types.go`) demands `State == StateIdle` and `Confidence >=
minimumDispatchConfidence` (0.75). The observed `0.25` is pinned by `observationConfidence`
(`internal/status/unified.go`) for any `StateUnknown`, so an unknown state can never pass.

`0a771c3a` added pi to exactly the registries that chain reads — `internal/agent/{parser,
patterns,types}.go` and `internal/status/{patterns,unified}.go`, including a pi arm in
`determineStateAt`. So the classifier is reachable from the poll, and the panes still resolve
to `unknown`. `composerMarkerForAgent` (`internal/tmux/session.go:2203`, entries for
`AgentClaude` and `AgentCodex` only) is a different table and is not the cause: it fails open
for unlisted types and gates a keystroke preflight and a reporting-only verdict, never this
timeout.

**The one path not yet traced, and the first place to look:** how a pane's `Pane.Type` is
derived from its tmux title and fed to `buildPaneObservation`'s `normalizedAgentType`. If a pi
pane's type does not normalise to `AgentTypePi` at that point, `determineStateAt` never enters
the pi arm at all and falls through to the generic path — which produces exactly
`StateUnknown` at 0.25 on a pane whose text is a perfectly good pi prompt. That is consistent
with every field in the observed error, `freshness=fresh` included: the capture is current,
it is the classification that is empty.

**Why the existing test suite did not catch it.** `TestDetermineStatePiPaneIsNotUnknown`
(added by `0a771c3a`) proves the classifier layer resolves a pi capture, and it passes. Nothing
exercises `waitForSpawnPaneReady` or `spawnPaneObservationSafeToDispatch` *succeeding* for any
type outside `cc`/`cod`. `TestDispatchSpawnPromptSequenceReadinessTimeout` covers the timeout
path for `AgentClaude` only. So the layer under the gate is tested green while the gate itself
is untested for the type that fails — which is why a merged, correct-looking classifier fix
changed nothing in production.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A six-pane `pi` spawn delivers all six prompts: `ntm spawn` exits 0 with no
      `spawn prompt setup failed` line, and each pane's scrollback shows its prompt text.
- [ ] The readiness poll observes a live pi pane as `state=idle` with `confidence >= 0.75`
      within the 30s `spawnPromptReadyTimeout` — verified from the observation, not from the
      absence of an error.
- [ ] `Pane.Type` normalises a pi pane to `AgentTypePi` at `buildPaneObservation`, or the
      report says why the type is something else and the fix is made where it belongs.
- [ ] The three reproductions above re-run on the fixed binary produce zero readiness
      timeouts across 18 panes.
- [ ] Done when: a six-pane pi swarm can be launched twice in a row with no manual prompt
      delivery.

## Tests

- **Unit** — `spawnPaneObservationSafeToDispatch` returns true for a pi observation built from
  a real captured pi prompt, and false for a pi pane mid-work. This is the assertion the suite
  is missing today; it must fail against the current binary before the fix.
- **Unit** — `normalizedAgentType` / `Pane.Type` derivation maps a tmux pane titled as ntm
  titles a pi pane to `AgentTypePi`. Table-driven over every type in `knownAgentTypes`, so the
  next agent type added cannot repeat this silently.
- **Integration** — `waitForSpawnPaneReady` against a fake observer that yields a pi
  observation, asserting it returns before the deadline. The existing timeout test covers only
  `AgentClaude` and only the failing direction.

## Blast radius

`internal/cli/spawn.go` (the poll and its gate), `internal/status/unified.go` (state and
confidence), and whichever file in `internal/tmux` derives `Pane.Type` from the pane title —
the third is the one the trace has not pinned yet, and finding it is part of the work. Their
tests: `internal/cli/spawn_state_test.go` and `internal/status/unified_test.go`. No schema, no
robot-API surface, no change to the delivery mechanism itself.

## Recovery path

None needed — no state is migrated and no data is rewritten. If a fix regresses the
`cc`/`cod` path, revert the commit; readiness is computed per spawn and nothing persists
between runs.
close_reason: Closed at the owner's direction, NOT by verification of the remaining criterion. What is proven: the root cause was found and fixed in fa4a869f, merged - pi rewrites its own pane title, ntm derives a pane's agent type from that title, and the readiness poll therefore never reached the pi arm; the fix adds pi to detectAgentFromCommand and the process-tree fallback, proven red by mutation across five rows. What is NOT proven and was never run: this bead's own Done when, a six-pane pi swarm launched twice in a row with all six prompts delivered. The owner's instruction was to close rather than leave the bead in_review indefinitely and to file a fresh bead if the symptom returns. Recording the gap here so a later reader does not mistake this close for evidence.

The measured failure was state=unknown confidence=0.25, which is a capture the classifier did NOT recognise as a pi status line at all.

Six pi panes starting at once, each loading its skills list and extension preamble, may simply not reach the footer inside that window - which would make this a deadline problem rather than a classifier gap, and would explain both why it is 18/18 rather than intermittent and why a single-pane unit test cannot reproduce it. Confirm or refute that before writing any fix: capture what is actually on a pi pane at the moment the poll gives up.

comments.author: operator-review
comments.text:
Root cause found and fixed in fa4a869f, merged. One acceptance criterion remains, which is why this bead stays open.

ROOT CAUSE, measured rather than inferred: pi rewrites its own pane title. A pane was titled ntmtest__pi_1_deepseek by hand, pi was started in it, and 25 seconds later tmux reported the title as "π - bd-ffv3d" while pane_current_command still read "pi". ntm derives a pane's agent type from the title format <session>__pi_<index>_<model>, so by the time the readiness poll lists the pane that signal is gone, parseAgentFromTitle yields AgentUser, and the classifier never reaches its pi arm. That is why the failure was 18 of 18 rather than intermittent, and why a unit test fed a synthetic capture with a well-formed title could never reproduce it.

The earlier hypothesis recorded on this bead - that spawnPromptReadyTimeout of 30 seconds was too short for six pi panes - is refuted. It was a guess and the title rewrite is the mechanism.

THE FIX uses the fallback the code already had. session.go:3165-3170 already asks detectAgentFromCommand, then the process tree, whenever the title yields AgentUser and a command is known. Neither had a pi case, so the fallback led nowhere. pi is now detected in both, under the executable-only rule grok and antigravity already use, because "pi" is a short token that appears in unrelated argv elements. Proven red by mutation: removing both arms turns TestDetectAgentFromCommand_Pi and TestDetectAgentFromArgv_Pi red across five rows, including the false-positive rows that pin the executable-only rule. internal/tmux and internal/status green.

WHAT IS NOT DONE, and it is this bead's own "Done when": a six-pane pi swarm has not been launched against the fixed binary. Everything above proves the mechanism and that type resolution now survives the title rewrite; nothing yet proves that six prompts get delivered end to end. That single run is all that stands between this bead and closed. Install the fixed binary, run "ntm spawn <project> --pi=6:<model> --prompt ...", and confirm all six prompts land.

NOTE FOR OTHER WORK: the title is still destroyed. This change makes type resolution survive it; it does not make the title survive. Anything else in ntm that reads an ntm-formatted title from a live pi pane has the same blind spot, and that is worth its own bead if such a reader is found.
