title: Converge the bespoke per-query session flags onto --session
description:
## Outcome

The six robot queries that scope by a session flag of their own read the shared `--session` flag
instead, and their bespoke flag names are gone. `--robot-mail` resolves its session the same way.
After this bead there is exactly one spelling of "which session" for every query that filters by
one, and no caller has to remember which query invented which name.

## Context

An inventory of the whole robot surface on 2026-08-23 counted **154** registered `--robot-*`
flags. They divide by session scope like this:

| bucket | count | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 4 | already read the shared `--session` (`internal/cli/root.go:4787`) |
| B | 50 | take the session as their own flag's value (`--robot-tail=proj`) |
| C | 8 | answer about per-session state and ignore `--session` |
| D | 86 | no session dimension at all |
| E | 6 | fleet aggregates, ambiguous |

This bead is bucket C minus one. Seven of the eight already filter by session — they just do it
under a name each query invented for itself:

- `--events-session` for `--robot-events` (`internal/cli/root.go:832`)
- `--attention-session` for `--robot-attention` (`:883`) and, reused, `--robot-digest` (`:917`)
- `--overlay-session` for `--robot-overlay` (`:1112`)
- `--md-session` for `--robot-markdown` (`:2550`)
- `--dismiss-session` for `--robot-dismiss-alert` (`:2824`)
- `--robot-mail` (`:1173`) takes no session flag at all: it reads a positional argument, or infers
  the session from the working directory or the surrounding tmux client

The eighth, `--robot-rano-stats`, has no session filtering of any kind and is its own bead.

Five names for one concept is the tech debt the repo's own `AGENTS.md` refuses ("Never create
compatibility shims… Just fix the code directly", and no backwards compatibility is owed because
the project has no external users). So the bespoke flags are **deleted**, not aliased: an alias
would leave six spellings instead of five and would be exactly the shim that file forbids.

The resolution machinery to converge onto already exists and is proven: the four bucket-A queries
resolve through `resolveRobotPipelineSession` / `resolveRobotTokensSession` /
`resolveRobotAlertsSession` / `resolveRobotPaletteSession` (`internal/cli/root.go:5387-5401`),
each falling back to `robotSharedSession` bound at `:4787`. Its precedence is covered by
`internal/cli/robot_session_flag_test.go:1-49`.

`--robot-mail` is the one that needs a judgement rather than a rename: its cwd and tmux inference
is a convenience worth keeping, so `--session` becomes the highest-precedence source and the
inference remains the fallback when no flag is given.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--robot-events`, `--robot-attention`, `--robot-digest`, `--robot-overlay`,
      `--robot-markdown` and `--robot-dismiss-alert` all resolve their session from `--session`
      through the same helper path as the four bucket-A queries (`internal/cli/root.go:5387-5401`)
- [ ] `--events-session`, `--attention-session`, `--overlay-session`, `--md-session` and
      `--dismiss-session` no longer exist: passing one returns `INVALID_FLAG` through
      `classifyRobotExecuteError` (`internal/cli/root.go:417-448`), and the near-miss hint from
      `suggestNearestFlag` (`:456-486`) names `--session`
- [ ] No alias, no deprecation shim and no hidden flag is left behind for the five removed names
- [ ] `--robot-mail` reads `--session` when it is given, and keeps its positional-argument, cwd
      and tmux inference unchanged as the fallback when it is not — precedence asserted in that
      order
- [ ] Every one of the six queries returns the same payload for a given session as it does today
      when that session is passed the new way — the change is the flag, never the answer
- [ ] A session named through `--session` that does not exist returns `success:false` with
      `error_code: SESSION_NOT_FOUND` for all six, matching the bucket-A behaviour
- [ ] The four bucket-A queries and their precedence test
      (`internal/cli/robot_session_flag_test.go:1-49`) are untouched and still pass
- [ ] Every reference to a removed flag name in the repository's own docs is updated in the same
      commit — `grep` for each of the five names comes back empty outside the changelog
- [ ] Done when: `ntm --robot-events --session <name>` answers for that session, and
      `ntm --robot-events --events-session <name>` returns `INVALID_FLAG` with a hint naming
      `--session`.

## Tests

**Unit tests**, table-driven, in the style of `internal/cli/robot_session_flag_test.go` (cobra
`ParseFlags` against a throwaway command):

- each of the six queries with `--session` → resolves to that session
- each of the five removed flag names → `INVALID_FLAG` plus a hint naming `--session`
- `--robot-mail` with `--session` → the flag wins over the positional argument and over the cwd
  inference
- `--robot-mail` with no `--session` → today's inference, unchanged (regression)
- an unknown session on each of the six → `SESSION_NOT_FOUND`

**Unit test over the flag registry**: enumerate `rootCmd`'s registered flags and assert none of
the five removed names is present — the case that fails if one is quietly restored as an alias.

No fuzz, property or golden tests are owed: the surface is flag parsing and resolution
precedence.

## Blast radius

`internal/cli/root.go` — the six dispatch branches named above, the flag declarations for the
five removed names, and the shared resolution helpers at `:5387-5401`. The payload functions in
`internal/robot/` are called with a session the same way they are today, so no query's output
computation is touched. `--robot-rano-stats` and the 50 bucket-B queries are out of scope, as is
the refusal rule for queries with no session dimension.

The five bespoke per-query session flags (--events-session, --attention-session, --overlay-session, --md-session, --dismiss-session) are deleted rather than aliased, and the six queries read the shared --session; an unknown -session flag now suggests --session by suffix rather than by Levenshtein, which could not reach it. Verified by mutation, since the agent resumed its own interrupted work and could not observe red first: disabling the suffix check turns all five rows of TestClassifyRobotExecuteErrorSuggestsSessionForRemovedSessionFlags red, and re-registering --events-session turns TestRemovedSessionFlagsAreGone red with 'still registered ... it must be deleted, not aliased'. internal/cli and internal/robot green after merging current main in. One acceptance criterion was refuted with evidence rather than satisfied: a valid-but-nonexistent session returns success with empty results, not SESSION_NOT_FOUND, which fires only on an invalid name - pre-existing behaviour identical to the bucket-A filters, so no test was written for a behaviour that does not exist.

title: Scope --robot-snapshot to one session with the existing --session flag
description:
## Outcome

A robot caller can scope `--robot-snapshot` to one session, spelled with the `--session` flag
that already exists, and a scope naming a session that is not there is refused with
`SESSION_NOT_FOUND` instead of answered with an empty success. The reported
`{"name":null,"panes":[]}` observation is settled — reproduced and fixed, or refuted and
recorded.

## Context

Two symptoms were reported from one session on 2026-08-22: `--robot-snapshot` has no way to
filter by session, and a near-miss flag failed **two different ways** — once with `INVALID_FLAG`,
once returning `{"name":null,"panes":[]}` with no error at all.

What the code says:

- There are roughly **140** `--robot-*` flags, declared as one block of
  `rootCmd.Flags().BoolVar/StringVar` calls beginning at `internal/cli/root.go:4118`. They all
  belong to a single flat command — cobra dispatches on which flag was set, through an `if`
  chain (`internal/cli/root.go:6346`).
- **`--robot-session` does not exist.** An exhaustive scan of every registered `"robot-…"`
  literal in `root.go` has no such flag. So `INVALID_FLAG` is the *correct* answer for it, and
  the near-miss machinery already helps: `classifyRobotExecuteError`
  (`internal/cli/root.go:417-448`) maps cobra parse errors to codes and `suggestNearestFlag`
  (`:456-486`) adds a Levenshtein "did you mean" hint.
- Session scoping exists, but unevenly. A shared root flag `--session`
  (`internal/cli/root.go:4787`) feeds **only four** robot queries —
  `--robot-pipeline-run`, `--robot-tokens`, `--robot-alerts`, `--robot-palette` — through their
  `resolveRobot…Session` helpers (`internal/cli/root.go:3396+`). Separately,
  `--robot-inspect-session=<name>` (`internal/cli/root.go:4548`) takes the name as its own
  value. Everything else ignores `--session` entirely.
- `--robot-snapshot` (`internal/cli/root.go:4128`) is documented as "Unified state: sessions +
  beads + alerts + mail" and covers **all** sessions. Its only filter is `--since`
  (`internal/cli/root.go:805-820`), which is delta pagination, not scope. This confirms the
  reported gap directly.

**The second symptom is the more interesting one and it is not yet confirmed.** A flag that does
not exist cannot produce a silent empty answer — pflag rejects it before any handler runs. No
producer of a literal `"name":null` alongside a `panes` array was found in the tree; the two
structurally closest types are `SessionInfo` (`internal/robot/robot.go:1563`) and
`InspectSessionOutput` / `InspectSessionDetail` (`internal/cli/tui_parity.go:339-365`), and
neither naturally serialises `name` as JSON `null`. The most likely explanation is that the call
passed the **valid** `--session` flag to a robot query that never reads it: parsing succeeds,
the filter is a no-op, and the answer describes an unintended scope. That is a hypothesis, not a
finding, and settling it is part of this bead rather than an assumption inside it.

There is precedent for exactly this class of defect in the session-flag area: ntm#214, where a
deprecation hint pointed at a flag that did not exist — the regression test for it is
`internal/cli/robot_session_flag_test.go:1-49`.

**Two decisions were taken before this bead was dispatched, and neither is open.**

1. **The scope is spelled `--session`** — the shared root flag at `internal/cli/root.go:4787`,
   reused. No new session flag is introduced, and `--robot-snapshot` joins the four queries that
   already resolve it through their `resolveRobot…Session` helpers (`:3396+`) rather than taking
   a name of its own the way `--robot-inspect-session` does. The precedent, the resolution
   helpers and the regression test all exist; a second spelling would be a second thing to keep
   true.
2. **The uniform refusal rule is not in this bead.** Classifying ~135 robot queries into
   honours-a-scope and does-not, and refusing `--session` on the second column, is a sweep over
   the whole robot surface rather than a change to one handler. It is `bd-5u429`, which depends
   on this bead because its hint text names the flag this bead makes work.

The envelope needed for a clean refusal already exists: `RobotResponse`
(`internal/robot/types.go:227-260`) carries `success`, `error`, `error_code` and `hint`, with
constants including `INVALID_FLAG` (`internal/robot/types.go:92`) and `SESSION_NOT_FOUND`
(`:86`). So this bead adds no new error vocabulary.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--robot-snapshot` accepts a session scope, and the scoped answer contains only that
      session's data while the unscoped call behaves exactly as it does today
- [ ] A session scope naming a session that does not exist returns `success:false` with
      `error_code: SESSION_NOT_FOUND`, not an empty success
- [ ] `--robot-snapshot` resolves `--session` through the same helper path as the four queries
      that already do (`internal/cli/root.go:3396+`), not through a second resolution written for
      this one query
- [ ] `--robot-session` keeps returning `INVALID_FLAG` with the near-miss hint, and the hint now
      names the flag that actually scopes the query the caller was reaching for
- [ ] The `{"name":null,"panes":[]}` observation is reproduced or refuted, and the finding is
      recorded on this bead — if it is a real code path, it is fixed here; if it was `--session`
      passed to a query that ignores it, that is recorded and left to `bd-5u429`
- [ ] The four queries that resolve `--session` today
      (`internal/cli/root.go:3396+`) keep their current resolution precedence, asserted by the
      existing test
- [ ] Done when: `--robot-snapshot --session <name>` returns that session and no other, an
      unknown name returns `SESSION_NOT_FOUND`, and the unscoped call is byte-identical to
      today's.

## Tests

**Unit tests** in the two conventions already present:

- flag parsing and resolution, in the style of `internal/cli/robot_session_flag_test.go`
  (table-style, cobra `ParseFlags` against a throwaway command): scoped snapshot accepted and
  filtered; unknown session → `SESSION_NOT_FOUND`; unscoped snapshot unchanged;
  `--robot-session` → `INVALID_FLAG` plus the near-miss suggestion; the four existing queries'
  precedence unchanged.
- envelope shape, in the style of `internal/robot/envelope_test.go` and
  `internal/robot/tui_parity_test.go:1177` (marshal/unmarshal round-trips rather than golden
  files): every new failure path serialises a complete `RobotResponse` with `success:false`, a
  non-empty `error_code`, and no partial payload alongside it.

No fuzz, property or golden tests are owed: the surface is flag parsing and JSON shape. The
inventory test over every robot flag belongs to `bd-5u429`, not here.

## Blast radius

`internal/cli/root.go` — the `--robot-snapshot` handler and its flag declaration (`:4118-4128`),
the `--session` resolution helpers (`:3396+`, `:4787`), and the error classification path
(`:417-486`) — plus the robot output type behind snapshot in `internal/robot/`. The error
constants in `internal/robot/types.go:86-92` are reused, not extended. The four queries that
already resolve `--session`, and `--robot-inspect-session`, keep their behaviour; the other ~135
robot flags are not touched by this bead at all — the rule that applies uniformly to them is
`bd-5u429`.

title: A Claude pane's account cannot be pinned per spawn, and the config suggests a way that cannot work
description:
## Outcome

A Claude pane's account can be chosen at spawn time, per pane, without editing a shared config
file. The config's own comment stops describing a mechanism that cannot work.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the suggestion in `~/.config/ntm/config.toml`: *"To spread panes across accounts, leave
   this line generic and pass the account per pane at spawn time instead:
   `ntm spawn llmux --cc=2 --pane-env CLAUDE_ACCOUNT='{pane}'`"*.
2. Write the launch template to consume it, e.g. `claude-account ${CLAUDE_ACCOUNT:-bianca} …`.
3. `ntm spawn <session> --cc 1:sonnet --pane-env CLAUDE_ACCOUNT=gmail`.
4. Read the account the pane actually runs under, from the process rather than the config:
   `tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/<pid>/environ | grep -E '^(SHALLOW_PROFILE|HOME)='`.
5. Observe the default, `bianca`, every time.

## Context

There is no account field in the launch template's data. `internal/config/templates.go:28-35`
exposes `Model`, `SystemPromptFile`, `PersonaName` and `ReasoningEffort`, and nothing else, so a
template cannot name an account through the documented variable set.

`--pane-env` cannot substitute for it either, and the reason is mechanical rather than a matter
of ordering that could be tuned: `prependSpawnPaneEnv` builds the command as
`KEY='value' command` — the shape is pinned by `internal/cli/spawn_test.go:102`, which asserts
`prependSpawnPaneEnv("codex", expanded) == "CARGO_TARGET_DIR='…' GOPATH='…' codex"`. A
`${VAR:-default}` written inside the template is expanded by the shell **before** the assignment
prefix takes effect, so it always resolves to the default. The suggestion in the config comment
therefore describes behaviour the code cannot produce.

**What this costs in practice.** Running one pane of a swarm on a different account is a normal
requirement — it is how a mixed swarm avoids putting every pane on one quota. With no per-pane
mechanism, the only route is to edit the shared `config.toml`, spawn, and revert immediately:
the pane's command line is already typed by then, so the revert cannot reach it, and with
`--auto-restart` off nothing re-reads the file. That works, and it leaves a window of about two
minutes in which any other session spawning a `cc` pane lands on the wrong account. A config file
edited as a spawn-time argument is a race by construction.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An account can be named per pane at spawn time — through a template variable, a dedicated
      flag, or an accepted `--pane-env` — without editing `config.toml`
- [ ] Two `cc` panes spawned in one command can carry different accounts, and the account each one
      actually runs under is verified from the process environment, not from the config
- [ ] Omitting the new mechanism keeps today's behaviour exactly: the account named in the
      template is used, so no existing config changes meaning
- [ ] If `--pane-env` is the chosen route, the expansion order is fixed so a template referencing
      the variable resolves to the passed value; a test asserts the composed command line, in the
      manner of `spawn_test.go:102`
- [ ] The comment in the shipped `config.toml` describes the mechanism that works, and the
      example in it is one that has been run
- [ ] Done when: spawning two `cc` panes with different accounts in a single `ntm spawn` gives two
      panes whose `/proc/<pid>/environ` name different profiles, with `config.toml` untouched
      throughout.

## Tests

- **Unit:** over the composition of the pane command line, asserting the account reaches it —
  the positive case, and the `${VAR:-default}` case that silently resolves to the default today.
- **Integration:** a two-pane spawn with two accounts, asserting each pane's environment.
- **Regression:** the exact form the config comment suggests must either work or no longer be
  suggested; a test pinning the documented example is what keeps those two in step.
- **Mutation, before it is trusted:** make both panes carry the same account and confirm the
  integration test fails. A test that only asserts "an account is set" passes against the defect,
  which does set one — the default.

## Blast radius

The spawn template's data set (`internal/config/templates.go`), the pane command composition
(`prependSpawnPaneEnv` and its call site in `internal/cli/spawn.go`), their tests, and the comment
plus example in the shipped `config.toml`. No change to session creation, to prompt delivery, or
to any other agent type's launch path.

title: Resolve the Go toolchain in the Makefile instead of trusting PATH
description:
## Outcome

`make build` compiles with the toolchain that `GOROOT` already points at, whatever `PATH` the
caller happens to have. A build started from a shell with a polluted or reconstructed `PATH`
no longer picks up a different `go` driver and fails with an error that names the compiler
instead of the environment.

## Context

`Makefile:15` sets `GO := go` and resolves it through `PATH`. Which `go` answers is therefore a
property of the calling shell, not of this repo — and on a machine with two Go installs the
mismatch surfaces as a compile error:

```
compile: version "go1.26.6" does not match go tool version "go1.26.6-X:nodwarf5"
```

**The mechanism is a crossed `GOROOT`, not a rejected build cache.** A version manager exports
`GOROOT` pointing at its own install. When `PATH` resolves `go` to the distribution's driver
instead, that driver honours the exported `GOROOT` and invokes the *other* toolchain's
`compile`, which refuses to work with a driver it does not match. Driver from one toolchain,
tool from another. Measured on this machine, with `GOROOT` set to the version-manager install:
`PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH go build ./cmd/ntm` on an unmodified tree emitted the error above for
`internal/profilerecord`, `unicode` and `internal/godebugs`, while the same tree built clean
with the version manager's `go`.

Because the message names `compile`, the first suspect is the diff under test. That is the
whole cost of this defect: the failure points away from its cause.

The shell-side cause of that particular `PATH` ordering has been fixed separately, which is
exactly why this bead exists rather than being closed by it: the Makefile still delegates the
decision to `PATH`, so the next environment that reconstructs `PATH` differently — a systemd
unit, a container, an agent harness with its own home, a fresh machine where the distribution
package is installed first — reproduces it. A build recipe that cannot be trusted from an
arbitrary environment is not a build recipe.

Rejected: documenting that callers must pass `GO=` explicitly. A note only works on a reader
who remembers to look, and the failure gives that reader no reason to look — it points at the
compiler. The fix has to be in the thing that runs, not in the thing that describes it.

Rejected: unsetting or overriding `GOROOT` in the recipe. `GOROOT` is not wrong — it names the
toolchain that should be used. The driver is the half that is wrong, so the driver is the half
to pin.

This repository is a fork, so the change is divergence carried through every rebase. That cost
is accepted: `?=` keeps the variable overridable, so an upstream or a caller that wants a
different toolchain still gets one, and the conflict surface is a single line.

## Steps to Reproduce

```sh
echo "$GOROOT"                   # set, pointing at a version-manager install
which -a go                      # more than one, from different toolchain builds
PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH make build   # the distribution go wins as driver
```

Fails with `compile: version "..." does not match go tool version "..."`.
`make build GO=<version-manager go>` on the same tree succeeds.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Makefile:15` resolves the toolchain without depending on `PATH` ordering, and falls back
      to a bare `go` when no version manager is present, so a clean checkout on a machine with
      exactly one Go still builds.
- [ ] The assignment uses `?=`, not `:=`: `make build GO=/some/other/go` still overrides it,
      and `GO=` on the command line wins over the computed default.
- [ ] `PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH make build` succeeds on a tree where the bare `go build` under the
      same `PATH` fails — the reproduction above stops reproducing through `make`.
- [ ] `./ntm --version` after that build reports the current `git describe` value, proving the
      `LDFLAGS` still interpolate and the change did not break the version stamp.
- [ ] Done when: the reproduction command in Steps to Reproduce exits 0 on a machine carrying
      both toolchains and an exported `GOROOT`.

## Tests

- **Manual, recorded in the closing comment**: the before/after of the reproduction command,
  including the failing bare `go build` on the same tree, so the guard is shown to be capable
  of failing rather than merely observed to pass.
- **Manual**: the fallback exercised with a `PATH` that contains neither the version manager
  nor its shims, asserting the recipe resolves to a bare `go`.
- **Unit is not owed here.** There is no Go code in this change and no test harness for the
  Makefile; claiming a unit test would be padding. The reproduction command is the test.

## Blast radius

One line in `Makefile`. No Go source, no test files, no CI configuration. `build`, `build-all`,
`install` and `install-user` all read the same variable, so they are covered by the same line
and none of their recipes changes.

title: Tests leave the tmux sessions they created behind
description:
## Outcome

A test that creates a tmux session removes it, so a finished run leaves the server holding
nothing it created. What survives a run is then evidence, not litter.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the suite against a tmux server you can inspect — `NTM_TEST_DECOY=1
   scripts/test-in-container.sh` puts one there for exactly this purpose.
2. List the server's sessions afterwards.
3. Sessions created by the run are still there. Observed 2026-08-28 on the private socket used for
   the `bd-wkq` verification: `test`, `quick-fallback` and
   `labelquick-1787895219753467544--dev` outlived the run that made them.

## Context

The names say where they came from — one carries a nanosecond timestamp, the pattern used by
tests that build a unique session name — so these are test fixtures whose cleanup did not run or
did not cover them.

**Why this is worth a bead rather than a shrug.** It is not the resource cost; three idle
sessions are nothing. It is that a leaked session is indistinguishable from a session someone
else is using, and the whole `bd-wkq` incident was about a run reaching a server it did not own.
Any future check of the form "did this run leave the server as it found it" has to treat these as
noise, which is the same weakening the container's known failures cause elsewhere. A cleanup
sweep that kills anything matching a fixture pattern would be the obvious fix and the wrong one:
pattern-matching against sessions somebody else may have named is how a sweep starts reaching
past its own run, and `sweep.go:83-86` already records an earlier version of that idea reaping
1528 roots.

The right shape is each test removing what it created, in a `t.Cleanup` that runs even when the
test fails — and the three names above are the trailhead for finding which ones do not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the three observed leaks is traced to the test that creates it, and that test removes
      its session in a cleanup that runs on the failure path too
- [ ] A full container run with a decoy leaves the server holding only the decoy — no session
      created by the run survives it
- [ ] The check is mechanical: the harness can compare sessions before and after and report any
      that appeared, so the next leak is found by a red run rather than by reading a list
- [ ] Cleanup targets sessions by the name the test itself created, never by a pattern that could
      match a session the run did not make
- [ ] Done when: session count before equals session count after, across three consecutive runs

## Tests

- Integration, in the container: sessions listed before and after a full run, asserted equal.
- Unit, per fixed test: the cleanup removes the session when the test fails, not only when it
  passes — exercised by forcing a failure, since a cleanup on the happy path only is the defect
  itself.

## Blast radius

The test files that create the three leaked sessions, and `scripts/test-in-container.sh` if the
before/after comparison lands there. No production code.

## Recovery path

Test-only. Reverting restores the leaks, which cost nothing to have.

title: Put the model each pane runs into its environment as AGENT_MODEL
description:
## Outcome

`ntm swarm` puts the model each pane runs into that pane's environment as `AGENT_MODEL`, alongside the `AGENT_NAME` it already exports, so a pane can label the bead it claims with the model that will implement it without anyone typing the alias into a prompt. A launch that cannot say which model a pane runs refuses, naming the pane, the same way it refuses a pane without a name.

## Context

`bd-fug` (closed 2026-08-30) made `ntm swarm` export `AGENT_NAME` and `GIT_IDENTITY_ENABLED` into each pane's environment at session and pane creation (`internal/tmux/session.go`, the `-e` flags on `new-session` and `split-window`), because the caller's environment is not what the panes get. The consuming system (`llm-workflow`, phase P0 of its plan) records which model implemented which bead so that a later compliance audit groups false-closes by model; until this bead lands the claim line in the marching orders carries the alias by hand (`--add-label model:<alias>`), which is typed once per template and wrong the first time a pane is relaunched with a different `--model`. `ntm` already knows the model per pane: it is the spec in `--cc=N:model`, `--agy=N:model` and the config's per-agent defaults, and the regression survey of 2026-08-27 recorded that a relaunched pane's transcript keeps a stale `modelId`, so the environment is the only place the truth can live.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every pane created by `ntm swarm` (and `ntm add`) has `AGENT_MODEL=<the model spec resolved for that pane>` in its environment, read back with `tmux show-environment -t <pane>` and from `/proc/<pid>/environ` of the agent process.
- [ ] A pane whose model cannot be resolved (no spec, no config default) makes the launch refuse before any agent starts, naming the pane, under the same guard `bd-fug` added for `AGENT_NAME`.
- [ ] The value is the alias as passed to the CLI (for pi through litellm, the `-kN`-suffixed alias), never a display name; the manual states the format.
- [ ] Done when: a swarm of two panes with different `--model` specs shows two different `AGENT_MODEL` values in `tmux show-environment`, and a launch with a pane lacking a resolvable model exits non-zero naming it.

## Tests

- Unit: the resolver from spec and config to `AGENT_MODEL`, including the no-spec-no-default case.
- Integration, real tmux on a test socket: the two-pane case in the done criterion; the refusal case.
- Golden: the environment keys a pane receives, so `AGENT_NAME` and `AGENT_MODEL` are asserted together.

## Blast radius

`internal/tmux/session.go` (the environment passed at creation), the swarm launch guard `bd-fug` introduced, `cmd/` where the model spec is parsed, the manual page for `ntm swarm`. No change to how models are chosen.

## Recovery path

An additional environment variable; reverting the commit removes it and the guard's new branch, restoring `bd-fug`'s behaviour exactly.

title: Swarm spawn confirms per pane that the marching orders arrived, retries once, then reports
description:
## Outcome

A swarm spawn confirms, per pane, that the marching orders actually arrived — a capture after
delivery shows the prompt landed (context meter moved / orders text visible); a pane whose
delivery cannot be confirmed is retried once and then reported, never left silently empty.

## Context

o62l shakedown, 2026-08-31: the rebalance spawned four pi panes; one (glm-k3) sat for an hour
showing only the pi banner at 0.0% context — the prompt was never delivered and nothing noticed.
Sibling of bd-q2a (which fixed readiness gating for no-classifier types); this is the delivery
half: readiness said go, delivery silently failed, and no read-back existed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After spawn delivery, each pane's capture is checked for evidence the prompt landed; a
  clean prompt-at-banner pane triggers one retry then a loud report.
- [ ] A pane that received its orders is never re-sent them (planted negative — a duplicate
  prompt to a working agent is its own damage).
- [ ] One mutation per criterion, red recorded.

## Recovery path

Read-back and retry only; the spawn path itself is unchanged.

title: locks list cannot be read without a second source
description:
## Outcome

`ntm locks list` answers the question it is asked. Its output states whose reservations were
queried and over what scope on the same line as the count, so "no active file reservations" cannot
be read as one agent's view when it is the session's, or the reverse.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `ntm locks list` → `Error: accepts 1 arg(s), received 0`. The session is required and the error
   names an arity rather than the missing thing.
2. `ntm locks list <session>` with no reservations held anywhere:

   ```
   No active file reservations (session scope)
   Agent: AmberCove
   Project: /home/gabriel/repositories/<repo>
   ```
3. Ask what that means. `No active file reservations (session scope)` followed immediately by an
   agent identity reads as *AmberCove holds none*; the querying caller wanted *nobody holds any*.
   Nothing in the output settles which was answered.

## Context

Observed at the moment it mattered, during an unattended run. A codex pane had stopped with
*"Blocked: reservation guard refuses required `src/domain/mod.rs` held by GrayCompass"*, and the
question was whether that reservation still existed. `ntm locks list` gave the right answer — it
had expired — and the output could not be trusted to mean that without a second source, so the
tracker was consulted instead (`br coordination status` showed the holder's bead already parked and
its pane idle) and the conclusion was reached around the tool rather than from it.

That is the whole defect: a correct answer that a caller cannot act on alone. It costs a second
command every time the question is asked, and the question is asked exactly when a pane is stuck,
which is when a second command is most expensive.

The arity error in (1) is smaller and the same shape: it names the argument count rather than
saying the session is required and how to name it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The count line states the scope and the querier together — enough that "no reservations" is
      unambiguous between *the session holds none* and *this agent holds none*
- [ ] Both readings are distinguishable in the non-empty case too: a listing shows whose
      reservation each entry is, and whether the listing covers all agents or one
- [ ] Running it with no session prints what is required and an example, not only an arity count
- [ ] The agent identity and project path remain available, since they are what makes a stale
      working directory diagnosable — this bead clarifies the framing, it does not remove context
- [ ] Done when: with one agent holding a reservation and another holding none, one invocation
      makes clear which agents were covered and which hold what, with no second command.

## Tests

- **Unit:** over the output formatting, for four cases — nothing held anywhere, something held by
  the querier, something held by another agent, and something held by both.
- **Regression:** the exact three-line output from the reproduction must not be producible in its
  ambiguous form.
- **Mutation, before it is trusted:** make the formatter always claim session scope and confirm the
  single-agent case fails. Every one of these assertions is about wording, and a test that greps
  for a word passes against a formatter that prints that word unconditionally, which is the easy
  wrong fix here.

## Blast radius

The output formatting of `ntm locks list` and its argument validation, plus their tests. The
reservation layer itself, its expiry, and every other `locks` sub-verb are read and not changed.

title: add does not print the pane id it created
description:
## Outcome

`ntm add` prints the pane id it created. The caller can address the new pane immediately, without
a second command to find out what was made.

## Context

Adding a pane to a running swarm reports three lines — the Agent Mail name, the pane registration
name, and the new total, `total 9 panes now` — and not the pane id. The id is the only handle that
addresses a pane reliably: `%NN` is server-global and survives every window and index change, and
in an eleven-hour unattended run every prompt delivery used one. Names are the treacherous half —
`tmux -t <session>` silently resolves to a *window* when a window name matches — so a caller that
has just created a pane has to run `tmux list-panes` to learn the one fact it needs.

The operation itself is the cleanest in the tool: adding a codex pane to a running nine-hour swarm
disturbed nothing, respected the model pin, registered with Agent Mail, and came up at a working
prompt with no trust dialog. This bead is about the last line of its output.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ntm add` prints the pane id of the pane it created, in a form a caller can pass straight to
      `--pane=` or to `tmux -t`
- [ ] Adding more than one pane in a single invocation prints every id, each associated with the
      agent it belongs to
- [ ] The existing three lines are preserved: the Agent Mail name, the registration name and the
      new total are all still there
- [ ] The machine-readable output, if the command has one, carries the id under a named field
      rather than only in prose
- [ ] Done when: adding a pane and sending to the id printed by that same invocation delivers to
      the new pane, with no `tmux list-panes` in between.

## Tests

- **Unit:** over the output builder, asserting the id appears for a single pane and for several.
- **Integration:** add a pane to a scratch session, parse the id out of the output, and send to it;
  assert the text arrives in that pane and not in another.
- **Mutation, before it is trusted:** print a hardcoded id and confirm the integration test fails.
  A test that only asserts an id-shaped string appears passes against a formatter that prints the
  wrong one, and the wrong one is a pane belonging to someone else.

## Blast radius

The result reporting of `ntm add` and its machine-readable form, plus their tests. Pane creation,
model pinning, Agent Mail registration and the session's own bookkeeping are unchanged.

title: idle agy still classifies busy and spawn still times out on a live pane (bd-q2a follow-up)
description:
## Outcome

An agy pane sitting at its input prompt classifies as idle and accepts direct assignment; spawn's readiness wait does not fail a pane that is in fact ready. The symptoms bd-q2a's fix targeted no longer reproduce.

## Steps to Reproduce

Both observed 2026-08-31, AFTER bd-q2a's fix (47bae3b0 "gate agy readiness on the state telemetry it prints") was built and running (orchestrator survey, regression section, effect: no_change):

1. Spawn agy panes; let one finish its task and return to its input prompt. `ntm assign --beads <id> --pane <agy pane>` → refused: "pane 7 is busy (state: working), use --force to override". Both agy panes, visibly idle at their prompt, refused assignment all run.
2. Spawn a session including a codex pane: recovery-context delivery timed out with "timeout waiting for pane %646 to become ready; failing signal: confidence=0.50 (want >= 0.75)", and spawn exited with an error while the panes lived on.

## Context

bd-q2a closed on making the telemetry read authoritative — and the telemetry is now authoritatively wrong for idle agy: the classifier tells idle from working incorrectly in BOTH directions for half the roster (idle agy = working; modal-wedged codex = idle, per bd-fiq). Mechanical routing (the loop's dispatch, direct assign) is impossible for those panes without --force, which discards the safety the state check exists for. This bead is the follow-up with the post-fix evidence; it should start from reproducing case 1 with the current binary.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An agy pane at its input prompt (fixture capture from the shakedown, or a live spawn) classifies idle within one classifier pass, and direct assign to it succeeds without --force.
- [ ] Spawn of a mixed session completes delivery to a pane whose readiness confidence is genuinely ambiguous, or fails ONLY that pane with the session left usable and exit code reflecting partial success — never an error exit with all panes alive and untagged.
- [ ] Done when: the two reproduction cases above, replayed against the new binary, both pass.

## Tests

- Unit: classifier golden tests from captured agy idle-prompt pane text asserting idle; integration: spawn readiness path with a stubbed low-confidence reader asserting the partial-failure contract.

## Blast radius

Confined to ntm's pane-state classifier (agy patterns/telemetry read) and spawn's readiness/delivery error path, plus their tests. No assign semantics change for panes that classify correctly today.

title: Five packages fail in the container for environment reasons
description:
## Outcome

Every test that fails in the container fails for a reason someone decided: either it is fixed, or
it skips with a stated precondition. `scripts/test-in-container.sh` becomes a run whose red means
something, instead of a run with a known noise floor nobody can distinguish from a regression.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `scripts/test-in-container.sh` from the repository root.
2. Five packages fail — `internal/checkpoint`, `internal/cli`, `internal/robot`, `internal/status`,
   `internal/tmux` — on a tree whose own gates are green.

Reproduced identically across four full runs on 2026-08-28, including three consecutive runs of
the same commit, so this is the container's steady state and not flakiness.

## Context

The container harness landed with `bd-wkq` because the suite had twice damaged its host. It works
for the question it was built for — a decoy session survives a full run there — but it arrived
with a set of failures that come from the environment rather than from the code, and nobody has
gone through them.

Three environmental differences are known and are the first things to check against each failure:

- **tmux 3.5a in the image against 3.7b on the host.** A behavioural difference between those
  versions is the single most likely explanation for a test that passes in a host package run and
  fails here.
- **No `br` and no `bv` in the image.** Tests that shell out to either get a missing binary rather
  than a tracker.
- **No network, and a fresh `HOME`.** Anything reaching a registry, a socket or a cached
  credential finds nothing.

Some of the named failures look like each of those. `TestInternalMonitor_*` (three of them, each
failing in under 0.01s) fail too fast to be doing any tmux work at all, which points at a missing
precondition rather than a behaviour. `TestRestorer_RestoreFromCheckpoint_*` take 28-39s before
failing, which points the other way. The point of this bead is that nobody has actually looked.

**Why it matters more than the count suggests.** A harness with a known noise floor is one people
stop reading. The suite already earned that treatment on the host, which is how it went from a
safety net to a thing that must not be run; a container run whose failures are "the usual ones"
is the same story starting again.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the five failing packages has every one of its container failures classified: fixed,
      or skipped with an explicit precondition naming what is absent
- [ ] A skip states the missing thing (`tmux >= 3.7`, `br`, network) rather than skipping on a
      generic "not supported here"
- [ ] Where the image can reasonably supply what is missing, it does — adding `br`/`bv` to the
      image is preferable to skipping tests that exercise them, and that trade is decided per tool
      and recorded
- [ ] `scripts/test-in-container.sh` exits 0 on a clean tree
- [ ] Done when: a red container run means something changed

## Tests

- Integration, the suite itself: a clean container run exits 0.
- Unit, for each skip added: the skip's condition is exercised, so a precondition that is always
  false — a skip that never runs the test anywhere — is caught rather than shipped.

## Blast radius

Test files under `internal/checkpoint/`, `internal/cli/`, `internal/robot/`, `internal/status/`
and `internal/tmux/`, plus `test.Containerfile` if a tool is added to the image. No production code. The guard from `bd-wkq` is not touched.

## Recovery path

Test-only, revertible per package. Adding a tool to the image changes only the image, which is
rebuilt from the file on every run.

title: internal-monitor outlives the session it watched
description:
## Outcome

Killing a session stops everything that session started. The resilience monitor does not outlive
the panes it watched, and relaunching under the same session name cannot leave two of them
running.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `ntm spawn <session> …` — this starts `ntm internal-monitor <session>` as a **sibling** process,
   not as a child of the session.
2. `tmux kill-session -t <session>:`
3. `pgrep -af "internal-monitor <session>"` → the monitor is still alive.
4. Relaunch a swarm under the same session name and repeat step 3 → two monitors, the elder
   watching a pane set it no longer owns.

Measured 2026-08-23 on a live session: after one kill-and-relaunch, `ps -eo pid,etime,cmd` showed
two monitors, the elder at 3h37m, its log carrying `Agent %265 crashed: Pane no longer exists`
six times over for panes that had been gone for hours. Observed again 2026-08-26 at the end of an
eleven-hour run: `pgrep -af "internal-monitor <session>"` returned a live pid after the session had
been killed, and it had to be killed by hand as a shutdown step.

## Context

The failure is quiet in both directions. A stray monitor spends its time reporting crashes for
panes that no longer exist, so its log fills with alarms that are all false — and a second monitor
started beside it watches the same session with no coordination between them. Neither condition
announces itself; the only way to find either is to go looking with `pgrep`.

It is documented as a trap rather than fixed: the operator's own manual pairs its recommended kill
line with a warning to check for strays and kill the old one in the same breath. That is the right
thing to write down and the wrong place for the fix to live — a documented manual step is one an
unattended run does not perform, and this is a tool that exists to be run unattended.

The process name carries the session name, which is what makes the workaround possible
(`pgrep -af "internal-monitor <session>"` finds every stray) and is also the shape a fix can use:
the monitor already knows which session it belongs to.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After `tmux kill-session -t <session>:`, no `internal-monitor` process for that session
      remains — verified with `pgrep`, not inferred from the absence of the panes
- [ ] Starting a swarm under a session name that already has a monitor does not produce a second
      one: either the existing one is adopted, or it is stopped first, and which one happens is
      stated in the output
- [ ] A monitor whose session has disappeared exits on its own within a bounded time, so a kill by
      any route — not only ntm's own — converges to no stray
- [ ] It stops logging pane-crash lines for panes that no longer exist; a vanished pane set is a
      reason to exit, not a reason to alarm
- [ ] The manual's warning is updated to describe the behaviour that then exists, rather than
      teaching a cleanup step that is no longer needed
- [ ] Done when: kill, relaunch, kill again, and `pgrep -af internal-monitor` is empty at each
      step, with no manual cleanup anywhere in the sequence.

## Tests

- **Integration:** the four-step reproduction, asserting on `pgrep` output after each step — this
  is a process-lifecycle defect and only a real process can show it.
- **Regression:** the kill-and-relaunch sequence must not produce two monitors.
- **Mutation, before it is trusted:** make the exit path unreachable and confirm the integration
  test fails. A test that asserts "no monitor after kill" passes against a monitor that never
  started, so the test must first assert one is running — the positive half is what makes the
  negative half mean anything.

## Blast radius

How `internal-monitor` is started by `ntm spawn` and how it decides to exit, plus whatever
adopt-or-replace check runs at spawn when a monitor for that session already exists, and their
tests. The monitor's watching behaviour while a session is alive is unchanged; no pane, prompt or
agent path is touched. `docs/tools/ntm.md`'s trap entry lives in a different repository and is
updated there.

title: Give the last fixed tmux session name a per-run suffix
description:
## Outcome

No test in the tree creates a tmux session under a name a person could plausibly be using.
`internal/robot/send_test.go` gets the same per-run unique suffix every other tmux-creating
test in the repo already carries, and a sweep confirms it was the last one without.

## Context

`internal/robot/send_test.go:155` assigns the bare literal `session := "ntm-send-render"`,
creates it at `:156`, and kills it from `t.Cleanup` at `:159-160`. It is the only unsuffixed
tmux session name found in the tree. Every other real-tmux test suffixes: `internal/robot/`'s
own `robot_test.go` uses `"ntm_test_bundle_privacy_" + time.Now().Format("150405")`,
`internal/tmux/session_real_test.go:23-25` has `uniqueSessionName`, and
`internal/pipeline/real_tmux_integration_test.go:378` and
`internal/tui/dashboard/real_tmux_integration_test.go:29` both append `UnixNano`.

Under working isolation this is harmless: the package's `TestMain`
(`internal/robot/robot_test.go:152-175`) sets an isolated `TMUX_TMPDIR`, so the name lives on
a private server where nothing else can hold it. It matters in exactly two situations —
when isolation is defeated, and when two runs of this package share one server, where the
second `CreateSession` collides on the name and the first run's cleanup kills the second
run's session.

This is deliberately a separate, smaller bead from the isolation-bypass one. The bypass is the
defect; this is the one place in the tree where that defect has a name to land on. Fixing
either without the other still leaves a real improvement, so they are not sequenced.

## Steps to Reproduce

```sh
tmux new-session -d -s ntm-send-render
```

title: Spawn delivery must not time out on a pane its own telemetry calls ready
description:
## Outcome

`ntm spawn`'s prompt delivery does not time out on a pane whose own telemetry says it is ready: the readiness gate and the observation it reads agree, an agy pane (no composer classifier) has a defined readiness path, and a delivery failure names which signal disagreed instead of just "timeout waiting for pane to become ready".

## Context

Measured on the agent-usage-book reference run spawn, 2026-08-30 (survey run-log 6db7d42b in llm-workflow): `ntm spawn agent-usage-book --cc 2:sonnet::gmail --cc 1:sonnet::primary --cc 1:opus::primary --cod 2:gpt-5.6-terra:high --agy 2` exited 1 with both agy panes undelivered: "spawn prompt delivery failed for agent 1: recovery_context readiness for pane %92: timeout waiting for pane %92 to become ready; last state=idle freshness=fresh confidence=0.95", alongside "⚠ pane %92 (agy): no-classifier - no composer classifier for this agent type". The pane was ready by its own telemetry (idle, fresh, 0.95 - above the 0.75 SafeToDispatch bar) and the gate still timed out; the operator re-sent the marching orders by hand. This is the opposite signature of the closed bd-3nv/bd-ffv3d (pi panes stuck at state=unknown, confidence pinned 0.25, structurally below the bar). Traced 2026-08-31: the step loop and failure wrap live in internal/cli/spawn.go (`dispatchSpawnPromptSequence`, error wrap at spawn.go:4073, timeout body from `spawnReadinessError` at spawn.go:6081); confidence comes from internal/status/unified.go (`observationConfidence`); the "no composer classifier" verdict is internal/tmux/session.go:2426 (`ComposerClassifierVerdict`) - and bd-3nv already flagged that this verdict and the readiness gate can disagree per agent type. The suspicion to confirm or refute: for an agent type with no composer classifier, the gate waits on a signal that will never arrive, while the state telemetry it prints is ignored.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `ntm spawn <session> --agy 2` (any mix including agy panes; ntm v1.26.0-170).
2. Observe exit 1 with "timeout waiting for pane %N to become ready; last state=idle freshness=fresh confidence=0.95" and the no-classifier warning for the same pane, with the pane visibly idle and usable in tmux.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The readiness gate's decision input is reconciled with the printed telemetry: a pane at state=idle/fresh with confidence >= the SafeToDispatch threshold is dispatchable by the gate, or the gate's reason for still refusing is named in the error (which signal, its value, its threshold).
- [ ] An agent type with no composer classifier has an explicit readiness path (fall back to the state telemetry, or a per-type readiness probe) instead of inheriting a wait on a classifier that does not exist; the no-classifier warning states which path applies.
- [ ] Done when: the reproduction above delivers to both agy panes on a clean spawn, and a genuinely unready pane (mid-boot, no prompt yet) still times out with the failing signal named.

## Tests

- Unit (Go): the gate's decision table for (state, freshness, confidence, classifier-present) including the no-classifier row; the error text carries the failing signal.
- Integration: one spawn with an agy lane on a scratch session, delivery asserted; one forced-unready pane asserting the named-signal timeout.

## Blast radius

Confined to the spawn readiness/delivery path in internal/cli/spawn.go, the readiness decision in internal/status/unified.go, and the classifier-verdict interplay at internal/tmux/session.go:2426; their tests. Pane spawning itself, the assign path and the state classifier are not touched.
close_reason: readiness gate takes the state telemetry alone for agent types with no composer classifier (agy/gmi/cursor); cc/cod/pi keep the parser double-check; timeout error names the failing signal with value and threshold; bonus: fixed pre-existing sessionTarget bug appending ':' to pane-ID targets (the TestDetectPaneLocalActivityIgnoresNoisyNeighbor red on main), pinned by a unit test; PR 44 merged; scoped go tests green, 2 remaining tmux fails identical on main; implemented by deepseek-v4-flash-max-k2 on attempt 3

title: the internal session monitor surfaces its detections or stops running
description:
## Outcome

The internal session monitor ntm starts at spawn either surfaces its detections where an operator can subscribe to them (the robot surfaces and/or the session's journal), or spawn stops starting it. A monitor whose output nobody can consume no longer runs.

## Context

Measured 2026-08-31 (orchestrator survey, machinery section): the monitor (pid 3931875, started by spawn) contributed nothing visible to the whole run. The codex boot modal, the agy feedback modal and the frozen pi pane all happened under its watch without a line reaching any surface the operator read; its log (`~/.local/share/ntm/logs/agent-usage-book-monitor.log`) was found only during an unrelated diagnosis and held entries from previous days' sessions plus its own restart banner. Its stated purpose — detect crashed/rate-limited agents, suggest respawns — is exactly what bd-3b9 (frozen process as pane state) and the swarm observation layer need, so the capability belongs on a readable surface or nowhere: a background process that watches and tells no one is cost without signal.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide and implement one: (a) monitor detections are published to a robot-readable surface (a `--robot-monitor` or fields in the snapshot) and logged one-line-per-detection into the monitor log with the session name and timestamp; or (b) spawn no longer starts the monitor, and the help/docs stop describing it.
- [ ] If (a): the three shakedown blind spots — an agent process gone, a pane wedged on a boot modal, a rate-limit death — each produce a detection entry in a test session.
- [ ] The monitor log, if kept, is per-session or clearly session-tagged, so one session's diagnosis never reads another day's entries as current.
- [ ] Done when: an operator can either subscribe to the monitor's detections through a documented surface, or the process no longer exists to wonder about.

## Tests

- Integration (branch a): kill an agent process in a test session and assert a detection appears on the surface within the monitor's interval; unit: log lines carry session tag.

## Blast radius

Confined to ntm's session-monitor component, spawn's startup of it, and the robot surface it publishes to (additive). No pane, tracker, or send behavior changes.

title: Six internal/cli tests fail: fake agent panes are refused by the PANE_AGENT_DEAD guard
description:
## Outcome

`go test ./internal/cli/` passes on `main` with a live tmux. The six tests whose fake agents are
refused by the `PANE_AGENT_DEAD` guard either keep a foreground process the guard recognises, or
stop pretending to be agent panes — and the guard keeps refusing delivery to a pane whose agent
CLI really has exited, which is the defect it was added for.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On `main`, with a working `tmux` binary, run `go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1` (no `-short` —
   every one of these tests skips under `-short`).
2. Six tests fail, each with a message of this shape:

```
PANE_AGENT_DEAD: pane 1.3 is titled ...__cod_1_test-model but its foreground
process is "zsh" (agent CLI exited to a bare shell); restart it with
--robot-restart-pane, or target the user pane for deliberate shell input
```

Observed 2026-08-24 at `main`. Proven pre-existing rather than introduced by recent work: the
same six were run against `main` and against an older commit, each extracted with `git archive`
into a separate directory, and they fail identically in both.

## Context

**The six, and the three different fixtures behind them** — this is not one fixture with one bug:

- `testAgentCatCommandTemplate` (`internal/cli/testmain_test.go:12-15`) backs
  `TestAgentLifecycleSpawnWorkKill` (`internal/cli/lifecycle_test.go:18`),
  `TestRunReassignment_ToPane_Success` (`internal/cli/assign_reassign_test.go:244`) and
  `TestRunRetryAssignments_PreservesPreviousFailReasonAndMetadata` (`:350`, sharing
  `setupReassignSession` at `:143`). With a model set it renders to
  `: 'test-model' >/dev/null && /bin/cat` — a two-command shell list, so the shell stays as the
  pane's foreground process, and `cat` exits on stdin EOF.
- `configureSessionTemplateFakeAgents` (`internal/cli/session_templates_e2e_test.go:435-440`)
  backs `TestSessionTemplateSpawn_Builtin` (`:21`) and
  `TestSessionTemplateSpawn_CustomUserTemplate` (`:129`). It renders
  `/bin/sh -c 'stty -echo; printf …; while IFS= read -r line; do … done'` — the interpreter itself
  is `sh`.
- `TestDirectAssignCLIReplayIsDurableAndBypassesChangedPreflight` (`internal/cli/assign_test.go`)
  shares nothing: it writes its own `#!/bin/sh` script, launches it with
  `tmux.DefaultClient.Run("new-window", …)` and hand-sets the title with
  `tmux.SetPaneTitle(paneID, session+"__cc_1")`.

**What the guard actually compares.** `Pane.AgentCLIDead()` (`internal/tmux/session.go:601`)
returns false immediately unless the pane's stored `Type` — derived from its NTM-format title — is
a real agent type; otherwise it lower-cases the pane's live `pane_current_command`, reduces it to
a basename, and tests it against the fixed set `bareShellCommands` = `{zsh, bash, sh, fish, dash,
ksh, tcsh}` (`internal/tmux/session.go:592-594`). The message is formatted by
`RefuseDeadAgentPane` (`internal/dispatch/dispatch.go:317-324`), reached from two call sites:
`TMUXDeliverer.Deliver` (`internal/dispatch/dispatch.go:330`) and the inline deliverer of
`newShellDispatchServiceWithGate` (`internal/cli/send.go:3812`), which is the path `assign`,
`reassign` and `retry` route prompts through.

So every fixture above is capable of presenting a bare shell as the pane's foreground process,
while the title says the pane holds an agent. That is exactly the shape the guard exists to
refuse — it is not misfiring, it is correctly describing fake agents that do not look like
agents.

**The guard is newer than the fixtures, and landed without them.** `PANE_AGENT_DEAD`,
`AgentCLIDead` and `RefuseDeadAgentPane` all arrived together in `6f23ca95` (2026-08-04,
"refuse delivery to agent panes whose CLI is a bare shell"). That commit touched
`internal/cli/send.go`, `internal/dispatch/dispatch.go`, `internal/robot/is_working.go` and
`internal/tmux/session.go` — **no test fixture**. `testAgentCatCommandTemplate` dates to March
2026 and `configureSessionTemplateFakeAgents` to July, so both predate it by months.

**Why this is worth fixing rather than tolerating.** The failures are quiet in the two places
people look and loud in the one place nobody has looked yet:

- They **skip under `-short`**. All six call `testutil.RequireTmuxThrottled` as their first
  statement (`tests/testutil/throttle.go:115-125`, which skips on `testing.Short()` at `:117-118`
  before checking tmux at all). The repo's own quick gate is `go test -short ./...`, so the
  standard local check never sees them.
- They **do run in CI**: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installs tmux (`:241-247`, `:301-302`, `:326`)
  and runs `go test -v -race -timeout=15m … ./...` at `:258` with no `-short`.
- **CI has never run.** `gh api repos/<fork>/actions/runs` reports `total_count: 0` — Actions is
  disabled by default on a fork and was never enabled. So the red is latent: it appears the day
  Actions is switched on, or the day this goes upstream.

Meanwhile the immediate cost is local and real: an unscoped `go test ./internal/cli/` already
fails, so a genuine new regression arrives inside six failures that everyone has learned to scroll
past.

**Three repair surfaces exist and none is half-built.** Reported so the work does not start by
re-deriving them:

- Make each fixture hold a foreground process the guard does not read as a bare shell — `exec` the
  loop or `cat` in place of the interpreting shell, and keep stdin from reaching EOF. Touches the
  three fixtures.
- Teach the guard about test panes. There is no existing env-var or flag hook in
  `AgentCLIDead` or `RefuseDeadAgentPane` to extend, so this is new production code whose only
  caller is the test suite — which is the option to justify hardest, not the one to reach for.
- Change what the tests target or assert. None of the six mistargets a pane today; each drives the
  pane it spawned, so this means changing the identity the test claims, not fixing a selection
  bug.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1` with a live tmux passes on `main`, with none of the six
      tests skipped to get there
- [ ] Each of the six is fixed at its own fixture: `testAgentCatCommandTemplate`
      (`internal/cli/testmain_test.go:12-15`), `configureSessionTemplateFakeAgents`
      (`internal/cli/session_templates_e2e_test.go:435-440`) and the inline script in
      `TestDirectAssignCLIReplayIsDurableAndBypassesChangedPreflight` — a fix that repairs one
      fixture and marks the others skipped does not satisfy this
- [ ] `Pane.AgentCLIDead` (`internal/tmux/session.go:601`) and `bareShellCommands` (`:592-594`)
      still refuse a pane whose agent CLI has genuinely exited to a shell — asserted by a test
      that spawns a fake agent, lets it exit, and expects `PANE_AGENT_DEAD`
- [ ] The `PANE_AGENT_DEAD` text and both call sites (`internal/dispatch/dispatch.go:330`,
      `internal/cli/send.go:3812`) keep their current behaviour for real panes
- [ ] If the guard gains any test-only accommodation, it is named in the commit body with the
      reason, and it cannot be reached in a production run — a code path whose only caller is the
      suite is a decision, not a detail
- [ ] The six tests fail before the fix and pass after it, demonstrated by running them at the
      parent commit, not asserted
- [ ] No test is newly gated behind `-short` or behind a tmux check that it did not already carry
- [ ] Done when: an unscoped `go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1` on a machine with tmux reports no
      failures, and a fake agent that exits to a shell still produces `PANE_AGENT_DEAD`.

## Tests

The six existing tests are the test: they already assert the behaviour, and the work is making
them exercise it again rather than writing new coverage.

**One new unit test is owed**, in the convention of the existing dispatch tests: a pane whose
title says agent and whose foreground process is a bare shell must still be refused with
`PANE_AGENT_DEAD`. Without it, the fix has no guard against being "corrected" later by loosening
`bareShellCommands` — which would silently restore the delivery failure the guard was added for.

**Regression check, run rather than reasoned**: the six at the parent commit fail, and at the fix
commit pass, on the same machine in the same session.

No fuzz, property or golden tests are owed: the change is fixture shape plus one assertion.

## Blast radius

The three test fixtures — `internal/cli/testmain_test.go:12-15`,
`internal/cli/session_templates_e2e_test.go:435-440`, and the inline script inside
`TestDirectAssignCLIReplayIsDurableAndBypassesChangedPreflight` in `internal/cli/assign_test.go` —
plus one new dispatch test. `internal/tmux/session.go` (`:592-594`, `:601`) and
`internal/dispatch/dispatch.go` (`:317-330`) are **read, not changed**, unless the work
deliberately takes the second repair surface, in which case the criterion above governs it. No
production behaviour changes for a real agent pane, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is not touched:
whether Actions is enabled on the fork is a separate decision from whether the suite is green.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #8 (merged as 166da4f2). Four tests failed on eaa34f9a, not six: bd-htr's PR #5 had already repaired the replay test and TestAgentLifecycleSpawnWorkKill passes in isolation. Two of the four presented as 'cod composer not visible' rather than PANE_AGENT_DEAD, because RefuseDeadAgentPane runs before ComposerReadyForDelivery and the cat fixture settles fast enough to dodge the first gate and trip the second. Fixtures repaired without touching the guard: sh replaced by awk in configureSessionTemplateFakeAgents, and a separate constant for the two reassign tests so the ~30 other call sites of testAgentCatCommandTemplate stay as they are. go test ./internal/cli/ passes unscoped with live tmux.

comments.text:
Attempt merged as 99179923 and REVERTED as da150367 the same session. It introduced a regression, and the reason it did is the finding that matters for whoever takes this next.

WHAT THE ATTEMPT DID: the three fixtures were changed to hand the pane a process that is not a shell - awk reading stdin in place of the `while read` loop - so the pane's foreground process stops being `sh` while the fake agent waits. That part works. Of the five tests failing with PANE_AGENT_DEAD, four passed afterwards.

WHY IT WAS REVERTED: a test that was green before the merge went red after it.

    --- FAIL: TestRunReassignment_TargetBusyWithoutForce
        assign_reassign_test.go:685: expected error code TARGET_BUSY, got "RESERVATION_REQUIRED"

Verified against the parent commit with git archive: the same test passes there. So it is a regression from this change, not a pre-existing failure.

THE FINDING, and it invalidates the one-fixture approach: testAgentCatCommandTemplate is shared by tests that need OPPOSITE pane states, and the composer markers are the thing that decides which they get.

- With `printf '❯\n›\n' && /bin/cat` the pane reads as a ready agent, the two reassign tests pass, and TestRunReassignment_TargetBusyWithoutForce fails - it needs the pane to look busy, and instead the flow walks past the busy check into reservation and returns RESERVATION_REQUIRED.
- With `exec /bin/cat` the pane has no markers, TargetBusyWithoutForce passes and TestSessionTemplateSpawn_CustomUserTemplate passes, and the two reassign tests fail with "expected success envelope".

Both were measured, one after the other, in the same worktree. There is no single value of that template that satisfies both groups, so the fix cannot be one template: the fixture has to be split so each test gets the pane state it is actually asserting about, while none of them presents a bare shell.

WHAT STILL STANDS from the attempt: the awk approach for configureSessionTemplateFakeAgents and for the inline script in TestDirectAssignCLIReplayIsDurableAndBypassesChangedPreflight is sound and cost nothing elsewhere. The reverted diff is recoverable from 99179923.

ALSO ESTABLISHED, and worth not re-deriving:
- The count is five, not six. Measured twice on a clean base.
- Three tests in this package fail only in a full-package run and pass in isolation - TestSessionTemplateSpawn_Builtin, TestAgentLifecycleSpawnWorkKill, TestAgentLifecycleMultipleAgents. Contention, not fixture-dead. Do not fold them in.
- TestDirectAssignCLIReplayIsDurableAndBypassesChangedPreflight stops failing for the PANE_AGENT_DEAD reason once its fixture is repaired, and then fails at PANE_BUSY for a different defect entirely. title: Decide whether --robot-inspect-coordination and --robot-restore take a session scope
description:
## Outcome

It is settled whether `--robot-inspect-coordination` and `--robot-restore` belong in the column
of robot queries that honour `--session` or in the column that refuses it, and the reason is
written down. Without this answer the classification sweep has two flags it cannot place, and a
sweep with a hole is a sweep whose enumeration test lies.

## Context

The 2026-08-23 inventory divided all 154 registered `--robot-*` flags by session scope. Every
bucket was decided from the code except two, and both are genuinely ambiguous rather than merely
unread.

**`--robot-inspect-coordination` (`internal/cli/root.go:2679`)** is keyed by `AgentName` alone.
Agent names here are NATO-phonetic and generated per session, so two live sessions can hold an
agent with the same name. Today the query answers about whichever one it finds. A session scope
would disambiguate — but it may be that agent names are meant to be unique fleet-wide, in which
case the collision is the defect and a scope is the wrong fix for it.

**`--robot-restore` (`internal/cli/root.go:2598`)** is keyed by a save-file path (`SavedName`).
The saved file may itself name the session it came from, so `--session` could mean three
different things: restore into that session, refuse when the file disagrees with it, or nothing
at all.

The other six queries in the ambiguous bucket were resolved: `--robot-snapshot` is `bd-jlv68`,
and `--robot-status`, `--robot-dashboard` and `--robot-terse` are one bead of their own. These
two are what is left, and each is a decision rather than a filter.

## Options

- **A · Both honour `--session`.** What changes: `--robot-inspect-coordination` disambiguates a
  repeated agent name instead of answering about an arbitrary one, and `--robot-restore` gains a
  target session. Cost: `--robot-restore` needs a rule for the case where the flag and the save
  file disagree, and that rule is a new behaviour nobody has asked for yet.
- **B · Both refuse `--session`.** What changes: both join the 86 queries with no session
  dimension, and passing `--session` to either is an error with a hint. Cost: the agent-name
  collision stays, silently — an inspect that answers about the wrong agent looks exactly like
  one that answers about the right one.
- **C · `--robot-inspect-coordination` honours it, `--robot-restore` refuses it.** What changes:
  the collision is fixed where it is real, and restore keeps being addressed by the artefact it
  restores from rather than by a session. Cost: the two neighbours in the same bucket end up in
  different columns, so the classification table has to carry the reason.
- **D · Fix the agent-name collision instead, and both refuse.** What changes: agent names become
  unique fleet-wide, which removes the ambiguity at its source rather than filtering around it.
  Cost: a change to name generation, which touches spawn and every surface that displays a name —
  much larger than the sweep that raised the question.

## What decides it

Are NATO-phonetic agent names intended to be unique across the whole fleet, or only within one
session? If fleet-wide, the collision is a bug and the answer is B or D; if per-session, the name
alone is not an address and the answer is A or C. The generation site and whether it consults
existing sessions is what settles it.

For `--robot-restore`, the second question is whether a saved file records the session it came
from. If it does, `--session` is at best a redundant assertion and at worst a contradiction to
resolve; if it does not, a target session is a real missing input.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the two flags is assigned to exactly one column — honours `--session` or refuses it
      — and the assignment is recorded on this bead
- [ ] The reason is recorded with it, including which of the two questions above decided it
- [ ] Any follow-on work the answer implies exists as its own bead before this one is closed
- [ ] Done when: the classification sweep can place both flags without asking anyone.

## Recovery path

Nothing is built here, so nothing is undone. If the answer proves wrong once implemented, the
follow-on bead it produced is what gets reverted, and this bead is reopened with the reason.
